Temporal measurability is handled by averaging the data over the time-grid intervals and using the stability theory of $L^1$-viscosity solutions. The limited regularity of the Hamiltonian is addressed through arguments from nonsmooth analysis, based in particular on Clarke's generalized differential calculus. We prove that the discrete solutions converge, up to some subsequence, to a solution of the MFG system. As a consequence, the numerical approximation also provides a constructive existence result. Under a monotonicity assumption on the coupling terms, we show that the solution to the MFG system is unique, implying the convergence of the whole sequence of discrete solutions. Finally, numerical experiments in one and two spatial dimensions illustrate the robustness of the method, including a linear--quadratic example with a running cost that is discontinuous in time and for which we compute an exact solution.

[708] arXiv:2610.28337 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Beyond a Single Sentiment Score: Topical and Affective Dimensions of Emoji Meaning on Twitter
Rohan James, Ioannis Christofilogiannis, Yuuv Jauhari, Shreya Shah, Gauri Pethkar
Comments: 12 pages, 4 figures, 8 tables
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Social and Information Networks (cs.SI)

Emoji are widely treated as compact affective tokens whose meaning is summarised by a single sentiment score. We argue that this picture is incomplete. From a corpus of 16{,}575 English tweets and a per-emoji metric we call \emph{stability delta} (within-class minus between-class cosine similarity of sentence embeddings), we show that emojis used in tightly clustered topical contexts also exhibit \emph{more} polarised crowd-sourced sentiment, not less. Validated against the Kralj Novak et al.\ (2015) sentiment lexicon, the central correlation is Spearman $\rho = +0.361$ (Holm $p = 0.015$, 95\% bootstrap CI $[+0.10, +0.59]$); against the independent Ferré et al.\ (2025) Spanish 13-emotion ratings, $\rho = +0.509$ ($p = 0.0003$). The result survives permutation testing, BCa bootstrap, leave-one-out jackknife, partial correlation controlling for emoji frequency, and Holm correction across a four-test family. Topical coherence and affective dispersion are distinct dimensions of emoji meaning. As a downstream check we report leakage-free five-fold cross-validation results for sarcasm classification on the Emoji Sarcasm Dataset; all three baselines (a gated multimodal architecture, fine-tuned BERTweet features, and fine-tuned RoBERTa features) score above 0.97 macro F1, indicating the dataset has saturating emoji-label cues. We frame the classifier as supporting evidence rather than the contribution.

[709] arXiv:2610.28339 [pdf, html, other]
Title: HistoLoop: Iterative Contextual Inference with a Looped Transformer for Histology-Based Spatial Gene Expression Prediction
Ziang Liu, Jie Liu, Shuai Li, Yigui Feng, Qinglin Wang
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Predicting spatial gene expression from H&E images offers a scalable complement to experimental spatial transcriptomics. However, despite progress in spatial context modeling, how to construct subsequent context from spot states updated by earlier contextual interactions remains underexplored. We introduce HistoLoop, a looped Transformer that formulates prediction as iterative contextual inference. At each refinement step, HistoLoop aggregates the current spot states into context tokens at the corresponding resolution, processes them with a shared spatial Transformer, and retrieves spot-specific contextual information through cross-attention. A memory-mediated update integrates this information into persistent spot states, which are then used to construct context at the next, finer resolution. Under the HEST-Bench HVG50 evaluation protocol, HistoLoop achieves the highest macro-averaged gene-wise Pearson correlation among the compared methods across six cancer-specific tasks spanning five organs in HEST-1K. Ablation studies support the importance of recurrent state refinement and reconstructing context from updated spot states at progressively finer resolutions. Expression-derived clustering further suggests that HistoLoop better captures spatially organized multigene patterns.

[710] arXiv:2610.28340 [pdf, html, other]
Title: DeclineCraft: A RAG Abstention Benchmark for Jointly Measuring Combined Retrieval and Parametric Knowledge
Atharva Thakur, Abulhair Saparov, Bruno Ribeiro
Comments: 38 pages, 28 figures, 12 tables. Code: this https URL
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Information Retrieval (cs.IR)

Reliable retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) requires recognizing when neither retrieved documents nor parametric knowledge supports an answer. We introduce DeclineCraft, a dynamic abstention benchmark whose unanswerable questions target Minecraft feature additions after a corpus cut-off, with audits of possible parametric exposure. Later cut-offs support evaluation of future models. Across 27 LLMs, we measure Correct Abstention Rate (CAR; how often models acknowledge insufficient knowledge on unanswerable questions), Answerable Attempt Rate and Answer Accuracy. We find that (1) single-shot retrieval significantly raises CAR in 38 of 40 configurations (model and thinking setting) versus no retrieval. (2) Iterative RAG, in which the model self-assesses its context and can request up to two further retrieval rounds, significantly lowers CAR versus single-shot RAG in 30 of 40 configurations (mean 46.4%), with little change in Answer Accuracy (68.5% to 69.3%). Adding query rewriting and reranking to hybrid (dense & sparse) retrieval lowers CAR for all 12 models tested. (3) Larger models answer more accurately (Spearman $\rho = +0.60$ with total parameters), but neither model size nor release date shows a significant association with CAR. (4) Without retrieval, enabling thinking on the same weights lowers CAR significantly for 8 of 13 models (by 14% points on average), and the responses shift from acknowledged uncertainty to premise denial.

[711] arXiv:2610.28343 [pdf, other]
Title: The GenAI Who Knew Too Little: Revisiting Transactive Memory Systems in Human GenAI Collaboration
Christian Meske, Tobias Hermanns, Florian Brachten
Comments: Full paper accepted and presented at the 20th International Conference on Wirtschaftsinformatik (WI 2025), Münster, Germany. To appear in the conference proceedings (Lecture Notes in Information Systems and Organisation, Springer). This version is the submitted manuscript prior to peer review
Subjects: Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC); Computers and Society (cs.CY)

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly transforming knowledge work, creating new collaborative dynamics that challenge tradi-tional human-human interaction patterns. This study investigates how Transactive Memory Systems (TMS) manifest in human-GenAI collabora-tion. Through qualitative interpretive interviews with 14 knowledge work-ers and thematic analysis, we identified distinct TMS manifestations across its three main dimensions: (1) regarding specialization, expertise recogni-tion exhibited asymmetry. Humans developed awareness of GenAI capabili-ties while GenAI demonstrated only temporary recognition of human exper-tise; (2) in terms of credibility, humans formed ambivalent trust relation-ships with GenAI, simultaneously attributing expertise to the latter while implementing additional verification processes; and (3) concerning coor-dination, where humans primarily directed more passive GenAI systems lacking initiative, resulting in hierarchical interaction patterns and unidi-rectional information flow. Our findings reveal that TMS manifests differ-ently in human-GenAI compared to human-human collaboration, necessitat-ing theoretical adaptations including trust markers, acknowledging GenAI's absent metamemory, and identifying its temporary memory.

[712] arXiv:2610.28346 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Auto-Director: Leveraging Multi-Agent Collaboration for Autonomous Video Editing
Yuxia Chen, Wenbo Zhu, Yangguang Ji, Zhenxiang Jiang, Teng Zhong, Yu Zhang
Comments: Accepted at MMM 2027
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Autonomous video editing from open-world resources remains a challenging problem in multimedia content creation. Retrieval-based methods are constrained by fixed source material and lack creative flexibility, while generative models struggle with long-horizon coherence and often diverge from user intent. Both paradigms fail to replicate the structured, multi-stage reasoning that underlies professional post-production. To address these limitations, we present Auto-Director, a tool-augmented multi-agent framework that mirrors professional editorial workflows: a Planning Agent decomposes abstract topics into fact-grounded scripts via retrieval-augmented planning; a Material Agent indexes open-world footage through shot segmentation and visual tagging; an Editor Agent assembles semantically aligned clips with MLLM-driven spatial adaptation; and a Critic Agent governs an iterative Reflect-and-Revise loop that checks scene-level alignment and pacing. To rigorously evaluate this new paradigm, we introduce VEdit-Bench, a benchmark of 100 expert-curated topics with human-annotated Golden Scripts and a five-dimensional metric suite covering Narrative Logic, Factual Accuracy, Semantic Alignment, Compositional Quality, and Stylistic Cohesion. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Auto-Director significantly outperforms baseline methods in both automated metrics and human evaluation, effectively bridging the gap between amateurs and professional-grade video production.

[713] arXiv:2610.28348 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Characterizing Cross-Relay Generalization Failure in Machine Learning-Based Power System Protection
Nithin Pradeep Nadayil Kizhakkethil, Julian Oelhaf, Christian Bergler, Andreas Maier, Siming Bayer
Comments: 6 pages, 3 figures. Accepted for presentation at the IEEE Power & Energy Student Summit (PESS 2026), Karlsruhe, Germany
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Machine learning-based fault detectors are often evaluated at the relay locations used for training, although local voltage and current measurements vary across power networks. This work investigates cross-relay generalization for binary detection of faults anywhere in the network using local measurements, rather than line-selective tripping. Using 50 ms windows from a simulated 110 kV transmission network, we evaluate a multilayer perceptron across all 64 source target combinations of eight relays and five random seeds. A shared simulation-level split and source-only threshold selection provide a controlled held-out evaluation without target-specific calibration. Despite nearly unchanged mean F1-scores (0.730 within-relay versus 0.734 cross-relay), the mean false-positive rate (FPR) increases from 0.088 to 0.341, while the mean false-negative rate decreases from 0.399 to 0.318. The change is strongly directional: models trained at Bus 2 relays yield a mean FPR of 0.670 at Bus 1 and Bus 3 relays, compared with 0.096 for cross-relay transfers within the same bus group. Linear probing indicates that learned representations retain coarse bus-group information, while exploratory class-conditional latent distribution analysis shows no consistent monotonic association with transfer errors. These findings demonstrate that aggregate metrics can conceal location-structured changes in false-alarm behavior, highlighting the importance of evaluating error types separately when assessing cross-relay generalization.

[714] arXiv:2610.28350 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Gated Prototype Transfer for Zero-Support Medical Vision Language Model
Sumaiya Fazal, Rizwan Qureshi, Laleh Behjat, Samira Ebrahimi Kahou
Comments: Accepted to Symposium on Model Accountability, Sustainability and Healthcare 2026
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Realistic few-shot adaptation of medical vision-language models (VLMs) can leave low-prevalence classes without any labeled support. The training-free SS- Text+ solver remains operational in this setting, but its zero-support prototypes receive no visual adaptation and fall back to a purely textual class prototype. We in- troduce Gated Knowledge-Guided Prototype Transfer (GProtoT), a pre-repulsion module that transfers supported-class visual residuals to missing classes using VLM similarity and an ontology-based clinical distance. A validation-free evidence gate scales transfer based on semantic relevance and residual agreement, thereby limiting unsupported extrapolation. In 50 paired realistic one-shot trials on MESSIDOR with FLAIR features, severe and proliferative diabetic retinopathy were absent from every support set. Relative to SS-Text+, gated ProtoT improved missing-class recall by 5.23 points, average class accuracy by 1.37 points, and the missing/supported recall harmonic mean by 1.83 points. It reduced negative- transfer frequency from 46-48% for ungated transfer to 2%, while at the cost of reductions of 1.20 percentage points in supported-class recall and 0.45 percentage points in top-1 accuracy. These results indicate that evidence-based gating provides a safety mechanism for the knowledge source. GProtoT is based on SS- Text+ and requires no gradients, validation data, or additional model inference, of- fering a low-compute path toward accountable adaptation under incomplete clini- cal supervision. Code is available: this https URL

[715] arXiv:2610.28351 [pdf, html, other]
Title: RayCo4D: Ray-Conditioned Continuous Motion Model for Monocular 4D Dynamic Reconstruction
Yuanxiang Ni, Xianliang Huang, Ruihan Hou, Feng Xie, Hao Zhang
Comments: 25 pages, 13 figures
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Reconstructing dynamic 3D scenes from monocular video requires inferring motion from noisy and intermittently visible observations. Long-range tracks provide valuable geometric constraints, but integrating their fragmented temporal coverage into shared, continuous motion remains challenging. We introduce \textbf{RayCo4D}, a ray-conditioned continuous motion model for monocular 4D reconstruction that explicitly separates visual measurements from latent 3D motion states. Each track is associated with a reference-time 3D query constrained to its camera ray, and its image and depth observations constrain shared latent motion nodes through local many-to-many associations. Each node maintains an $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ pose and body-frame velocity at sparse support times. A white-noise-on-acceleration process prior couples neighboring states and defines continuous-time interpolation, allowing observations across visibility intervals to jointly constrain the same latent state this http URL inferred shared motion is transferred to Gaussian primitives through dual-quaternion blending, while reference-anchored local $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ residuals capture fine-scale non-rigid deformation beyond the shared scaffold. Experiments on diverse monocular dynamic scenes show that RayCo4D achieves competitive novel-view synthesis quality, improves structural and temporal consistency under rapid motion and incomplete tracks, and supports continuous-time rendering.

[716] arXiv:2610.28354 [pdf, html, other]
Title: S-Agent 2.0: Spatial Reasoning with a General Coding Agent
Rui Gong, Ruoyu Wang, Yalun Dai, Hao Li, Sidi Yang, Qihao Zhao, Hongyu Li, Zeyang Guan, Fangzhou Hong, Zhaoxi Chen, Kim-Hui Yap, Ziwei Liu
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Spatial reasoning asks a model to work out where objects are in 3D space, how they relate to one another, and how they move. Agentic VLMs have recently brought large improvements on such tasks by letting the model actively gather evidence with 3D perception tools instead of answering in a single pass. Even so, on many questions the tools return the right evidence and the model still does not arrive at the correct answer: the gap between model and tools, where raw readings become usable conclusions, is left unfilled. We present S-Agent 2.0, a spatial reasoning agent that equips an off-the-shelf general coding agent with a command-line perception toolkit, and we design the interface around one principle: help the VLM close the evidence loop: acquire scene evidence, remember it in a persistent scene memory, and interpret each reading in plain spatial language. This design keeps the full flexibility of a coding agent, and every reading it acts on stays grounded in the tools' geometry. On MMSI-Bench and ReVSI, the toolkit improves a strong open-source model, Qwen3.8-27B, by +13.9 and +20.5 points over the same agent without tools, and a strong closed-source model, Gemini-3.8-Flash, by +11.2 and +9.6 points. With the open backbone S-Agent 2.0 reaches 66.5 on MMSI-Bench and 82.3 on ReVSI, ahead of the specialized system SpatialClaw on the same backbone (62.6 and 74.5), and with Gemini-3.8-Flash it reaches 74.1 and 90.5 against its 67.0 and 79.7. Both tool gains shrink as the backbone grows more capable, but SpatialClaw's shrinks far more on ReVSI, from +13.2 to +2.7, while ours stays at +9.6. S-Agent 2.0 also works across different general coding agent harnesses, such as Codex and Claude Code.

[717] arXiv:2610.28355 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Beyond the Point Mass: Acceptance-Derived Weights and Distributional Losses for Speculative Decoding
Tianyu Wu, Zhuohan Wang, Jonathan Geuter, Yu Yao, Weifan Jiang, Chengxi Zhang, Ju Li, Minlan Yu
Comments: Code: this https URL
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

In speculative decoding, a lightweight draft model proposes tokens that the target model verifies in parallel, speeding up generation without changing the target distribution. D-PACE (Wu et al., 2026) trains such drafters with a loss that weights each position by its contribution to the expected accepted length. Both its weights and its cross-entropy (CE) loss use only the draft's probability of the recorded target token, treating the target as a point mass. Under rejection sampling, however, a sampled draft token is accepted with probability equal to the overlap of the draft and target distributions, one minus their total variation (TV). We derive D-PAL (Dynamic Position-wise Acceptance Loss) from the exact expected accepted length, using this overlap as the acceptance signal. This yields overlap-based position weights with log acceptance (LA) as the per-position loss, and the objective reduces to D-PACE for a point-mass target. Since the weights are detached, any per-position loss can replace LA in practice. We show that forward KL divergence and Rényi divergence of order 1/2 match or exceed LA, and that Rényi-1/2 provably bounds the true acceptance rate from above and below. Replacing CE with Rényi-1/2 improves acceptance length under both D-PACE's weights and ours. On six benchmarks with a Qwen3-4B target, D-PAL raises mean acceptance length over D-PACE from 4.50 to 4.57 at T=0 and from 4.20 to 4.28 at T=1, and consistently achieves higher throughput at both temperatures.

[718] arXiv:2610.28356 [pdf, html, other]
Title: CountVideoBench: A Benchmark to Evaluate Prediction Biases on the Object Counting task by Video-Language Models
Marc Chapus, Carlos Crispim-Junior, Véronique Eglin, Atilla Baskurt
Comments: Accepted at BMVC 2026. Project page: this https URL
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Object counting in videos remains a poorly characterized capability of multimodal large language models. Counting questions are included in many existing VideoQA benchmarks, but the ground-truth count distributions in these benchmarks are heavily skewed toward small values. Across the nine benchmarks we survey, the median ground-truth count is at most five, and the three most frequent values together account for between 45% and 93% of the videos. The resulting mean accuracy is then dominated by the most frequent counts; a value-dependent bias at a rare count contributes negligibly to the average and remains invisible. We introduce CountVideoBench, a benchmark of 2,600 synthetic videos covering 26 cardinalities in the interval [5, 50] (100 videos each), grouped into six clusters of consecutive counts that span the range while enabling near-neighbor comparisons. Each video contains a single class of static objects under a controlled camera motion, removing object motion and reducing recognition as confounds. We evaluate sixteen video-language models from nine architecture families in a zero-shot setting. No model exceeds 27.6% Exact Match. The dependence of accuracy on cardinality varies across models, ranging from monotonic decline to a non-monotonic peak-and-collapse pattern, which rules out increasing difficulty with cardinality as the dominant explanation of counting failure. Every model further concentrates its predictions on its own set of preferred integers, with accuracy peaks coinciding with these values and collapsing at adjacent counts. These findings highlight the need for balanced, diagnostic counting benchmarks to reliably assess this fundamental visual capability.

[719] arXiv:2610.28361 [pdf, html, other]
Title: FALCA: Falsification-Aware Reinforcement Learning with Hierarchical Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Deep Search Agents
Zijun Dou, Kun Luo, Chaofan Li, Shuqi Lu, Zheng Liu
Comments: 19 pages, 20 figures, 2 tables. Project page: this https URL
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Long-horizon deep search requires LLM agents to iteratively decompose complex information needs, gather evidence from external sources, and maintain a reliable research state under multiple constraints. A central challenge is that early mistakes can be amplified over the search trajectory: agents may anchor on an incorrect candidate, collect partially supporting evidence, overlook contradictions, and accumulate errors that misguide subsequent reasoning. We propose FALCA, a falsification-aware framework that formulates deep search as a propose-falsify process. FALCA adopts a collaborative Searcher-Falsifier architecture, where the Searcher proposes candidate answers or sub-answers, while independent Falsifiers actively seek counterevidence, check unmet constraints, identify conflicts, and produce concise falsification reports for research-state revision. To strengthen this loop, we introduce falsification-aware training, combining SFT warmup on falsification trajectories with agentic RL based on parallel rollouts and hierarchical credit assignment over research stages, state transitions, and actions. Experiments on five search benchmarks show that FALCA improves long-horizon deep search performance over backbone and harness ablations, while reducing confirmation bias and error accumulation through more effective falsification and research-state revision.

[720] arXiv:2610.28362 [pdf, html, other]
Title: SPAR: Search-trained Push Action Ranker for Efficient Navigation Among Movable Obstacles
Dhruv Metha Ramesh, Tri-An Nguyen, Junshan Huang, Jingjin Yu, Kostas E. Bekris, Abdeslam Boularias
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO)

Navigation Among Movable Obstacles (NAMO) requires a robot to rearrange objects that block access to its goal. For a pushing robot, progress may depend on a setup push that enables a later opening without itself clearing a passage. The number of candidate sequences can grow exponentially with sequence length, making physics-based search costly. We introduce the Search-trained Push Action Ranker (SPAR), which learns to prioritize push primitives from simulated search outcomes. Searches over sequences of up to two pushes per object provide supervision that distinguishes immediate openings from setup pushes. A transformer trained with regression and ranking losses scores primitives using contact tokens conditioned on scene geometry and reachability regions. The same model guides simulator evaluations in SPAR Search and selects actions for direct execution in SPAR Policy. Both modes solve successive keyhole problems that open access to neighboring free-space regions within a NAMO planner. Across successful runs on $300$ simulated two-push keyhole problems, SPAR Search reduces median simulator calls by $7.0\times$, leading to a $3.8\times$ reduction in planning time relative to Random Search. Without retraining, the same ranker guides search on $600$ keyhole problems which have no solution within two pushes. At a depth limit of five pushes, SPAR Search achieves $50.7\%$ success within $100$ simulator calls, compared with $20.2\%$ for Random Search. These gains carry over to NAMO planning: on hard simulated scenes, SPAR Search achieves $47\%$ success within $100$ simulator calls, compared with $21\%$ for Random Search. In real-robot experiments, SPAR Policy succeeds in $37/40$ trials without a physics-based digital twin, compared with $33/40$ for SPAR Search and $27/40$ for Random Search.

[721] arXiv:2610.28363 [pdf, html, other]
Title: TexFlow: learning crystallographic texture on SO(3) manifold via normalizing flows
Gowtham Nimmal Haribabu, Tarakram Ramgopal, Divakar Vetriveeran, Siddhant Kumar
Comments: 43 pages, 18 figures
Subjects: Computational Engineering, Finance, and Science (cs.CE); Materials Science (cond-mat.mtrl-sci)

Crystallographic texture is an important microstructural feature that statistically describes the orientations of grains in polycrystalline materials. Conventional texture analysis relies on the orientation distribution functions and pole figures, which are essential for interpreting the texture of a given material specimen but do not, by themselves, provide a direct framework for predictive modeling of process-structure-property linkages. Data- and machine learning-based approaches offer a means to address this gap; however, a key challenge lies in developing representations and learning frameworks that account for the manifold structure of rotations. In particular, many existing machine learning techniques are designed for Euclidean data and therefore are not readily applicable to rotations in the non-Euclidean group $\text{SO}(3)$. Here we introduce TexFlow, a conditional normalizing flow framework for texture modeling that learns a probability distribution over rotations in $\text{SO}(3)$ by construction. Rotations are encoded in a six-dimensional Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization representation which is then mapped back to valid rotations $\mathbf{R}\in\text{SO}(3)$. The framework supports conditional probabilistic modeling of texture $p(\mathbf{R}|c)$, where $c$ may represent processing parameters like temperature or deformation state. To complement conventional texture-analysis visualizations, such as pole figures and sections of the orientation distribution function, we further introduce Hopf-fibration visualizations as a compact global representation of texture. TexFlow is validated on both unconditional and conditional experimental and simulated texture datasets spanning diverse material systems. We show that TexFlow can accurately capture multimodal textures and their conditional evolution, providing a data-driven framework for establishing process-texture linkages.

[722] arXiv:2610.28364 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Context-Aware Prompt Injection Detection via Small Language Models in RAG Pipelines: nokast-secureRAG
Abhishek Rai
Subjects: Cryptography and Security (cs.CR); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Local Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection and retrieval poisoning, where malicious instructions in retrieved content are mistaken for trusted input. We present nokast-secureRAG, a roughly 0.5B-parameter small language model that acts as a semantic firewall between retrieval and generation. It jointly evaluates the user query and retrieved context, classifying the pair as safe, suspicious, or malicious. The model is trained using a teacher-judge-student pipeline: a 35B teacher generates 5,233 examples across four attack families, and an independent 120B judge re-labels them, achieving 95.0% agreement before student fine-tuning. On a held-out in-distribution test set, the model achieves 0.994 detection recall at a 0.026 false-positive rate and a 0.006 attack-success-rate proxy, outperforming a regex baseline, a public prompt-injection classifier, Llama Guard 3 1B, and its untuned version. Prompt-Guard-86M reaches 0.900 recall but has a 0.690 false-positive rate. On a judgment-flip test, where the same sentence is benign or malicious depending on context, the model correctly classifies both cases 75% of the time, outperforming the compared baselines. Ablations indicate that retrieved context carries the main attack signal, while query-context consistency reduces false positives. Single-request latency is 293-404 ms, above the target of 100 ms, while amortized throughput latency is 37 ms under batching. On the external PoisonedRAG benchmark, recall falls to near zero, indicating that fluent fact-poisoning attacks lie outside the detector's instruction-consistency threat model. We report this limitation alongside the in-distribution results. The model, data-generation pipeline, and evaluation harness are released open source.

[723] arXiv:2610.28366 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Relative Representations Enable Portable White-Box Monitoring Across Language Models
Tim Bakker, Christos Louizos
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Independently trained autoregressive language models often acquire similar capabilities, but it remains unclear whether their internal representations organize behaviorally relevant information in compatible ways. We show that models do in fact organize information similarly by using specific behavioral probes that operate on compatible representations. This unlocks portable white-box monitoring: a probe developed and validated on one model can be reused when the model changes, without requiring labeled target data. To overcome incompatible native activation coordinates, we express each example through its angular distances to a shared set of anchors. We introduce a global anchored construction that summarizes information from all transformer layers and removes model-specific layer selection, so the same frozen probe can be straightforwardly applied to another model. We evaluate cross-model probe transfer across monitoring tasks on trivia datasets, safety monitoring, and mathematical reasoning. On average, transferred global anchored probes preserve at least 85% of same-model probe AUROC over chance. Anchored probes also support transfer to related datasets, remain robust across model scale and prompt changes, and retain performance better than standard probes after model updates. Transfer is nevertheless task- and target-dependent and can fail even when the monitored property remains strongly decodable in the target model. Overall, global anchoring reveals substantial task-relevant compatibility across independently trained models and provides a practical basis for portable white-box monitoring.

[724] arXiv:2610.28369 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Don't Skip the Baseline: A Controlled Comparison of Dynamic Expert Skipping in MoEs
Jakob Steimle, Thomas Elsken, Daniel Ehrhardt, Lukas Rinder, Daniel Cremers, Xi Wang
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

A growing body of work proposes dynamic expert-skipping methods for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models that adjust the number of experts activated per token during inference, aiming to preserve model quality while further reducing the number of active parameters. These methods have added calibrated importance scores, inter-expert similarity metrics, or learned per-token allocators in order to identify experts to skip. However, different calibration regimes, different reductions in the effective number of experts, and evaluation suites make comparisons difficult. We classify four representative prior methods into a unified taxonomy and benchmark them against a natural, simple baseline: statically reducing the number of experts $k$ (i.e., same reduced $k$ across all layers and tokens). We provide a fair comparison of these methods at matched expert-compute budget, on two modern MoEs (Gemma4-26B-A4B and Qwen3-30B-A3B) in a text-only setting and a contemporary vision-language model (Qwen3-VL) in a multimodal setting. Surprisingly, we find that the simple baseline is hard to outperform consistently across models, modalities, benchmarks, and calibration settings. The methods we benchmark often underperform the baseline and achieved gains, when present, are minor. We further find that the effective $k$ achieved (or optimized for) in calibration can diverge from the effective $k$ in testing, resulting in over- or under-estimating the compute at inference time. Based on these findings, we recommend a calibration-free per-modality static $k$ reduction and validate this on a held-out model and modality. We further argue that a static control at matched measured compute is the baseline any dynamic skipping method must beat.

[725] arXiv:2610.28370 [pdf, html, other]
Title: A General Construction of Strict Models in HoTT
Niyousha Najmaei, Niels van der Weide
Subjects: Logic in Computer Science (cs.LO); Programming Languages (cs.PL); Category Theory (math.CT)

Homotopy type theory (HoTT) provides a natural setting for studying the metatheory of type theory, as it comes with additional extensionality principles compared to ordinary Martin-Löf type theory. In particular, it is especially suitable for developing semantics of type theory, where one distinguishes two kinds of models: strict models, which give us sound interpretations, and pseudomodels. Pseudomodels are useful as they occur prevalently and can be turned into strict models by constructions called strictifications. However, the commonly used strictifications do not translate well to HoTT, as they require assumptions that are generally not satisfied by concrete examples of models.
We show how to carry out the universe model construction, due to Voevodsky, in HoTT. Under this construction, every pseudomodel together with a universe type closed under enough type formers gives rise to a strict model. We also show how to interpret type formers in the resulting model assuming that the universe is closed under them. Finally, we demonstrate that this construction generalises existing instances of strict set models in the literature, and we apply it to more examples, yielding presheaf models and assembly models of type theory in HoTT. Our results are formalised in Rocq using the UniMath library.

[726] arXiv:2610.28372 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Fast and scalable multi-GPU sliced FFT solvers for asymptotically compatible discretizations of 3D nonlocal diffusion problems
Yulong Li, Jiale Meng, Zhenlin Guo, Jiwei Zhang
Comments: 26 pages, 8 figures, 6 tables
Subjects: Numerical Analysis (math.NA)

Large-scale 3D peridynamic transient diffusion simulations are constrained by the computational cost and memory requirements of nonlocal interactions. We propose a fast and scalable multi-GPU sliced FFT algorithm based on the recently developed asymptotically compatible finite difference (ACFD) scheme. By exploiting the discrete operator's structure and finite interaction range, the algorithm combines FFT acceleration with local inter-GPU communication. It preserves the ACFD scheme while avoiding the global data redistribution required by full 3D FFTs. We build a matrix-free GPU conjugate gradient (CG) solver, use multigrid preconditioning to reduce iteration counts, and introduce a human-audited configuration agent for efficient cross-level configuration. Strong-scaling tests show that sliced FFT-CG achieves 93.2% parallel efficiency on eight GPUs, compared with 28.2% for full FFT-CG on the same problem and hardware. The framework supports approximately 10.29 billion degrees of freedom on eight RTX 4090 GPUs with 24 GB of memory each. The insulated penny-shaped cutout benchmark demonstrates transient simulation with approximately 8.58 billion degrees of freedom. Three-dimensional star-shaped interface evolution further demonstrates convergence toward the local solution in a nonlinear phase-field problem. These results demonstrate that sliced FFT provides a scalable multi-GPU approach for fast computation of 3D peridynamic diffusion.

[727] arXiv:2610.28380 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Object-Oriented Harness: Evolving Agent Harnesses through Object-Oriented Design
Gaotang Li, Bhavana Dalvi Mishra, Yifei Ming, Yanfei Chen, Zhongying CuiZhu, Lesly Miculicich, Long T. Le, Rui Meng, Chun-Liang Li, Hanghang Tong, Chen-Yu Lee, Tomas Pfister
Comments: 20 pages, 10 figures
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Software Engineering (cs.SE)

Agent harnesses are executable code that specifies the prompts, tools, and control flow around a language model. A single global harness can struggle with heterogeneous tasks that require different execution strategies. In this work, we introduce Object-Oriented Harness (OO-Harness), a harness optimization framework that evolves a hierarchy of executable harness classes using object-oriented design. During training, an evolution agent uses execution records to create a family of specialized harnesses, each implemented as a subclass of the base or an existing specialized harness via inheritance. At test time, a harness router uses routing lessons accumulated during training to select a specific harness for each task. Across three long-horizon benchmarks spanning business workflows, workspace tasks, and tool use, OO-Harness achieves the best performance among the compared methods, with an absolute improvement of up to 15% over the base. Extensive ablation studies examine the contributions of its core components.

[728] arXiv:2610.28381 [pdf, html, other]
Title: CAPSafe: A Benchmark for Contextual Action and Plan Safety Reasoning in Embodied Agents
Youmna Farag, Svetlana Stoyanchev, Simon Keizer, Mohan Li, Rama Doddipatla
Journal-ref: REALM 2026
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Reasoning about safety is essential for embodied agents powered by large language models (LLMs). We introduce the Contextual Action and Plan Safety benchmark (CAPSafe), designed to evaluate safety reasoning at two levels: (1) an action-level dataset that tests whether a single action is safe given its environmental context, and (2) a plan-level dataset that evaluates whether agents can generate safe long-horizon plans for complex hazardous household tasks. CAPSafe models safety conditions where hazards are situational (inferred from object properties), multiple hazards can co-occur within the same environment, and each is annotated with a relative severity level for fine-grained analysis. Evaluating nine closed and open-source LLMs reveals a substantial gap between hazard recognition and safe long-horizon planning. Several models achieve high accuracy in recognizing unsafe actions (exceeding 90% in the best cases), yet safe long-horizon planning remains substantially harder. Gemini-3-pro achieves the highest safe success rate (78.19%), while other models remain below 65%. These results highlight that robust safety reasoning over long action sequences remains an open challenge.

[729] arXiv:2610.28382 [pdf, html, other]
Title: RACE: Learning Multimodal Search through Referential Abstraction and Compositional Evidence
Eric Tao, Minhao Sun, Liyan Liu, Zhijing Wu, Xiaohan Yu, Lang Mei, Li Huang, Chao Feng, Jinchao Ma, Sichen Kang, Siyu Mo, Chong Chen
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Training multimodal search agents requires tasks that make visually grounded search necessary for determining the answer. Textual identity clues and unused target evidence allow shortcuts in synthetic questions, weakening supervision for visual search and evidence integration. We propose RACE, an image-conditioned task synthesis framework that constructs dependencies from images to targets and from target-specific evidence to answers. Referential Abstraction (RA) replaces identity-revealing text with specific visual references or ambiguous relational references resolved by searching among depicted candidates. Compositional Evidence (CE) links retrieved facts about multiple entities in one image or entities from different images into joint questions whose answers require every designated contribution. Both operations also apply to images found during search, allowing new visual observations to determine subsequent search targets or supply answer evidence. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-27B on only 12K teacher-generated trajectories from RACE raises average accuracy across ten multimodal benchmarks from 53.5 to 56.0, a relative improvement of approximately 4.7% over the matched base agent. Our code, data, and model will be publicly available.

[730] arXiv:2610.28385 [pdf, html, other]
Title: RACE: RoPE-Aligned Attention Compression Based on Query-Key Activation Energies
Irene Tenison, Abdulrahman Alabdulkareem, Daniel Karl I. Weidele, Nima Dehmamy, Dan Gutfreund
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Head-dimension compression can reduce the memory required by the key-value (KV) cache, but existing methods often reconstruct full-dimensional representations during inference, adding significant decoding FLOPs overhead. We formalize the design considerations for converting pretrained attention into a natively reduced-dimensional form that reduces both KV-cache storage and attention computation using a calibration set. Specifically, we consider reductions that (1) apply a shared projection to queries and keys so that they remain in a common reduced feature space, (2) derive this projection jointly from query and key activations to better preserve their interaction, and (3) are compatible with the pretrained RoPE transformation. To obtain a reconstruction-free realization of this reduction, we restrict it to coordinate selection and theoretically show that RoPE compatibility then holds if and only if complete rotary pairs are retained. Building on this characterization, we introduce RACE, a post-training method that selects rotary pairs using their joint query-key activation energy. We theoretically show that this criterion minimizes a separable, calibration-dependent upper bound on post-RoPE query-key product approximation error. The resulting reductions are folded into the model weights and require neither runtime reconstruction nor specialized kernels. Across three model families and different compression levels, RACE outperforms structured pruning and remains competitive with reconstruction-based methods on language-modeling, zero-shot, and long-context tasks. At 50% KV-cache retention and 256K context, RACE reduces total inference FLOPs by 47.8%, yielding 1.79x higher throughput, 43.2% lower time-to-first-token (TTFT), and 28.1% lower allocated GPU memory in comparison to an uncompressed model.

[731] arXiv:2610.28386 [pdf, html, other]
Title: VisualEvolve: A Skill Self-Evolution Framework for Visual Reasoning
Jiawei Wang, Yucun Li, Xueqi Li, Shenghao Wang, Xinquan Gong, Dan Zhang, Zheqi Lv, Yuquan Le, Shaozu Yuan, An Zhang, Da Cao, Tat-Seng Chua
Comments: 29 pages, 9 figures. Project page: this https URL
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Visual tool use enables vision-language models (VLMs) to acquire task-relevant evidence, but its effectiveness can be limited by predefined visual operations and the tool-use strategies learned during training. Representing these operations and strategies as reusable external skills allows them to be refined through self-evolution without updating model parameters. However, skill refinement can introduce performance regressions. Meanwhile, inspecting accumulated task execution trajectories together with skill evolution history may lead to evolution evidence overload. To address these challenges, we propose VisualEvolve, a self-evolving framework that evolves executable visual operations and tool-use strategies for VLMs through a Select--Execute--Evolve--Evaluate cycle. Skill-Library Snapshot Selection uses performance on a fixed validation set disjoint from execution tasks to select an effective historical snapshot for subsequent evolution, limiting the propagation of performance regressions. Progressive Evidence Access (PEA) guides capability-gap diagnosis through a coarse-to-fine hierarchy comprising the Skill-Performance Report, Evolution Log, Trajectory Summaries, and relevant raw trajectory segments. Across four VLM backbones and six evaluation sets from three benchmarks, VisualEvolve improves over the Initial Skill Library in 23 of 24 settings, with a maximum gain of 15.1 percentage points on VisualProbe Hard using Qwen3.5-Plus. Ablation studies support the contributions of Snapshot Selection and PEA, while further experiments show that skills can be improved using experience from different data settings and directly reused across backbones. Moreover, VisualEvolve enables effective skill self-evolution with over an order of magnitude fewer task-solving trajectories than estimated for representative RL-based methods.

[732] arXiv:2610.28388 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Self-Credit: Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Agentic RL via Intra-group Rescaling
Fangcong Yin, Ming Yin, Tanvi Bhandarkar, Aashu Singh, Eryk Helenowski, Shlok Kumar Mishra, Saghar Hosseini, Karthik Abinav Sankararaman, Greg Durrett, Dinkar Juyal
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

LLM agents are commonly trained with RLVR, but the sparse nature of typical RLVR rewards makes credit assignment challenging, especially for long-horizon tasks. We propose Self-Credit, an end-to-end agentic RL method that creates dense supervision signals from sparse outcome rewards using self-generated credit assignment via intra-group rescaling. Self-Credit builds on group-based RL with three components. First, during its rollouts, the policy model generates summaries with citations to earlier turns containing critical evidence, which serve as self-generated credit. Second, we refine this model-generated credit with intra-group rescaling, which compares cited actions across successful and failed rollouts for the same prompt. This approach uses group-level agreement and disagreement to remove undeserved credit and further emphasize credit assigned to critical actions. Third, advantage reweighting uses the rescaled credit weights to update the advantages of the cited turns. On BrowseComp-Plus, Self-Credit improves over the base models by 37.0 and 36.2 points on Qwen3 8B and 32B respectively, and outperforms the strongest agentic RL baselines by 8.5 and 5.6 points, respectively. Self-Credit also improves over the strongest baselines by 4.9 points on GAIA and 4.7 points on xBench-DeepSearch. Analyses show that self-generated credit provides useful signals for selecting critical actions, and that intra-group rescaling, especially on failed rollouts, is important across model scales.

[733] arXiv:2610.28392 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Budgeted Admission from Timestamped Capacity Records in Shared Clusters
Andrew Bond, Syed Izhan Khilji
Subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Probability (math.PR)

A cluster admission gate can receive a capacity record that no longer matches current schedulability. We study one exogenous binary schedulability unit under a bound on the joint probability of admission and unavailability. For a symmetric Markov state, we derive the stationary admission frontier for a fixed observation delay and apply finite likelihood allocation to a delay-tagged delivered record. A one-sided exact binomial endpoint calibrates each fitted policy, and exact enumeration confirms the per-policy confidence target in every tested parameter cell. A separate deterministic guard charges every unresolved admission against the realized allowance and bounds unavailable-state admissions at every prefix under truthful outcome feedback. An executable admission procedure composes the allocation and guard. The controlled system binds source sampling, NATS delivery, randomized admission, Kubernetes objects, and API-derived outcomes in one append-only record. Independent audit finds no missing event, identity mismatch, or state mismatch in the completed functional block. A separate CPU request-accounting check preserves Job and Pod identity across an unschedulable-to-complete transition.

[734] arXiv:2610.28393 [pdf, html, other]
Title: When Copying Is Hard: Copy-Constrained Decoding for Exact Span Reproduction
Jinghui Zhang, Lang Gao, Zongfang Liu, Ruihong Zeng, Zirui Song, Rui Yan, Kentaro Inui, Xiuying Chen
Comments: NeurIPS 2026
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Precisely reproducing a target span verbatim within a long context is a fundamental capability test for LLMs: even when the target string is present in context, models often still drift within the span or fail to stop correctly, revealing limitations in source grounding and boundary control. This capability has broad practical relevance. For instance, code generation often requires embedding sensitive strings such as API keys exactly as they appear in context. In this work, we construct a benchmark to test exact span reproduction ability across contracts, scientific literature, code, and random sequences, and find that current models still make surprisingly frequent errors. To address this, we propose CopyGen, a lightweight copy-constrained plugin for frozen LLMs that turns copying from a byproduct of next-token prediction into a controlled process. Our key idea is to decompose copying into three distinct decisions: when to copy, how far to copy, and when to stop. Concretely, CopyGen first determines whether to enter copy mode, then predicts a tentative copy length, and finally verifies the generated span token by token. During verification, we adaptively adjust the logits of copy continuation tokens to incentivize or suppress continuation, and emit only the longest valid prefix. Across three LLM backbones and four benchmark tasks, CopyGen improves average exact match by 35% relative without model finetuning, and integrates seamlessly with SFT to further improve it by 4%, while substantially accelerating generation. These results suggest that reliable exact copying is not something LLMs obtain for free, but a decoding-time control problem that requires explicit modeling. Code is available at this https URL.

[735] arXiv:2610.28397 [pdf, html, other]
Title: MAS-Guard: Unified Guardrails from Individual Agents to Multi-Agent LLM Systems
Mohammad Kachuee, Phu Mon Htut, Sheng Li, Nikolaos Pappas, Miguel Ballesteros Martinez, Yassine Benajiba, Sujith Ravi, Dan Roth
Subjects: Cryptography and Security (cs.CR); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Agentic AI extends large language models (LLMs) from generating responses to planning and executing complex workflows, substantially expanding their utility while exposing applications to unsafe actions, information leakage, and adversarial manipulation. Multi-agent systems further expand these capabilities through specialization and collaboration, but distributed authority, heterogeneous roles, and opaque or potentially compromised participants make safeguarding even more challenging. Existing defenses address important individual threats but provide fragmented coverage across local execution, system-level interactions, and enforcement mechanisms. We introduce MAS-Guard, a unified framework that closes this gap for safeguarding single- and multi-agent AI applications containing both instrumentable and opaque agents. Within instrumentable agents, the proposed local Agent Guardrail (A-Guard) layer applies task-specific experts to assess agentic events. At the system level, developer-owned Agent Charters and a Control Plane combine deterministic structural checks of routes, agent capabilities, and message formats with semantic assessments of roles and message content. These complementary layers enable enforcement through a shared set of interventions: allow, reflection, confirmation, and block. Evaluated across six benchmarks covering diverse single- and multi-agent scenarios with three agent LLMs from different providers, MAS-Guard reduces the overall attack success rate by 71.5-86.3% relative to unguarded agents, while meeting the utility reference criterion on benign tasks.

[736] arXiv:2610.28401 [pdf, html, other]
Title: SPECTER: Covert Data Exfiltration from Air-Gapped Systems via USB Power Modulation
Hyeongjun Choi, Ji Hyuk Jung, Ji Won Yoon
Comments: 11 pages, 7 figures, 3 tables
Subjects: Cryptography and Security (cs.CR)

We present SPECTER, a post-compromise covert channel that uses host-side USB power control to exfiltrate information from air-gapped and network-segregated systems. A transmitter with administrative privileges encodes bits through USB power-management or device-state operations without placing the payload in USB data transfers. The resulting signals are recovered through three alternative receiver paths based on smartphone charging states, visible peripheral behavior, and near-field RF activity. Experiments on Windows 10 and Ubuntu 22.04 demonstrate the channel on commodity hardware, with charging-state signaling at 0.2-0.25 bit/sec across Android and iOS devices and peripheral-state signaling at 1.0 bit/sec using a USB mouse on Windows. RF reception is demonstrated using a software-defined radio with a loop antenna in direct contact with the USB cable. Channel availability and observable side effects depend on the host configuration, connected device, and receiver path. These results identify host-side USB power control as a mechanism for low-rate exfiltration of short secrets and motivate treating USB power-management and device-state events as security-relevant telemetry.

[737] arXiv:2610.28402 [pdf, html, other]
Title: StreamEval: Evaluating Interactive Streaming Video Generation Models
StreamEval Team
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

As streaming video generation advances, enabling real-time interaction with generated video is becoming increasingly important. We introduce StreamEval, a unified benchmark for interactive streaming video generation spanning five tasks: avatar dialogue, avatar performance, world generation, instruction editing, and reference editing. StreamEval comprises 300 scripted test cases lasting 15-300s, each specifying initial assets, incrementally arriving multimodal requests, and explicit requirements for state changes and content preservation. Performance is assessed along four evaluation dimensions: task execution, state consistency, visual fidelity, and audiovisual coordination, instantiated through ten task-specific metrics on a 0-100 scale. Evaluating 37 distinct models across 300 test cases, we find that high visual quality and identity retention do not necessarily coincide with reliable request execution or sustained state consistency. In particular, request execution remains challenging: the highest task-specific scores are 36.90 for Following among seven avatar-performance models, 25.93 for Following in text-conditioned world generation, and 15.00 for Edit Success among three reported reference-editing models. These findings identify reliable request execution under timing and preservation constraints as a central challenge for advancing omni-modal real-time interactive systems. The leaderboard is available at this https URL

[738] arXiv:2610.28405 [pdf, html, other]
Title: DIVE: Benchmarking Full-Duplex Interaction with Visual Engagement in Continuous Streams
Yuhang Chen, Guangyue Liu, Shilong Liu
Comments: Preprint. 19 pages, 4 figures
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have substantially improved spoken interaction and video understanding. Existing online and streaming benchmarks primarily assess causal multimodal perception through timestamped question answering, whereas real-world interaction requires models to continuously identify task-relevant multimodal cues and decide whether, when, and how to respond. This leaves open how well current models can sustain real-time interaction throughout an evolving multimodal stream. To address this gap, we introduce DIVE, a benchmark for evaluating full-duplex interaction with visual engagement under continuous and realistic multimodal streams. It organizes six tasks into three complementary interaction scenarios. (1) Proactive Intervention evaluates whether models can identify emerging visual or semantic cues and intervene at the appropriate moment. (2) Continuous Engagement evaluates sustained participation through continuous visual tracking and visually grounded query interaction. (3) Interaction Coordination evaluates how models coordinate listening and speaking under overlapping and multi-party interactions. DIVE contains 525 audio/video samples with fine-grained human annotations and precise temporal metadata. Its evaluation protocol separates response quality, participation decisions, and response timing. We evaluate representative real-time models using response quality, window response rates, and reaction latency. Experiments show that leading real-time models achieve sub-second average response latency, yet their average window response rates remain at or below 53.77%. Response quality varies substantially across models and tasks, with adapting ongoing responses to newly arriving information remaining particularly challenging. We hope DIVE facilitates progress toward more natural and capable real-time multimodal interactive systems.

[739] arXiv:2610.28407 [pdf, html, other]
Title: The Instruction Tax on Factual Recall: Base Models Can Beat Their Instruction-Tuned Counterparts
Christophe Khalil, Aya Mourad
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

We present our solution to the AKBC LM-KBC 2026 Shared Task, where we achieved a score of 0.6836 on the official leaderboard, more than double the baseline of 0.2964. This task requires generating all possible objects for subject-relation pairs using a language model with up to 32 billion parameters, with no retrieval or fine-tuning involved. We show that the prompting methodology is as important as the model architecture: while the instruction-tuned model version achieves 0.5681 with its chat interface, the base model achieves 0.6836 when prompted using text completion. Thus, instruction tuning decreases factual recall; we refer to this effect as the instruction tax, which is caused by the model's weights rather than the prompting method. Our final solution is fairly straightforward: we prompt the base model with some examples from the training data, generate 64--256 outputs, and retain only the repeated ones. Two specialized methods are then applied for each relation: one improves the recall of large answer sets, and the other verifies a person's vitality before predicting their place of death.

[740] arXiv:2610.28409 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Rewards for Budget-Aware Multi-Turn Agents That Adapt to Arbitrary Test-Time Constraints
Tom A. Lamb, Adam Golinski, Eleonora Gualdoni, Sinead Williamson, Michael Kirchhof
Comments: 32 pages, 8 figures
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Large language model agents are often given an inference budget and asked to maximise success within it. A multi-turn agent has to allocate this budget across many environment interactions. An external harness can enforce the budget, but it remains unclear whether the agent itself can learn when and how much to spend. We ask whether agents can learn this allocation across dynamically specified budgets and which rewards best teach this behaviour. We adapt existing length penalties to budget constraints spanning multiple resource types, introduce new reward formulations, and compare eleven objectives in a shared training pipeline. We train Qwen3.5 models at 4B and 9B on AppWorld with budgets over tokens, API calls, and environment steps, and on the BabyAI gridworld with turn budgets. We train a separate policy for each environment and resource type, with each policy trained across budget values. Training with rewards that penalise overspending substantially improves within-budget success and natural compliance over untrained models and over training on task success alone, with agents learning to adapt their resource use to stated budgets and task difficulty. These gains extend to unseen budgets and, zero-shot, to a shifted task distribution and a new benchmark. Reward objectives trade off success within budget and natural compliance. A sigmoid penalty for overspending most often achieves the highest within-budget success at an individual budget, while a fixed negative reward for overspending generally yields the strongest natural compliance. Combining penalties for overspend frequency and magnitude gives the smallest average gap to the best method at each budget. Overall, we show that a single agent can learn to allocate resources across turns and adapt its behaviour to user-specified budgets using budget feedback without external budget-allocation controllers.

[741] arXiv:2610.28410 [pdf, html, other]
Title: A Multi-Agent Framework for Automated Machine Learning with Evidence-based Planning for Medical Image Analysis
Yiqing Shen, Mathias Unberath
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Deep learning has become the default tool for medical image analysis, driven by the open-source movement. However, achieving the best performance on a given task remains difficult, with architecture selection and hyperparameter optimization (HPO) still considered "more of an art than a science". Automated machine learning (AutoML) automates parts of model training, yet helps little in medical imaging: general-purpose approaches lack medical architectures and preprocessing, and medical-focused ones demand engineering expertise and remain confined to narrow tasks such as 3D segmentation. We introduce MedicalMLOmni, a multi-agent AutoML framework that automates model training for diverse single- and multi-modal medical tasks through a natural language interface. Specifically, MedicalMLOmni performs evidence-based planning by retrieving published results to guide model selection and configuration, and employs parallel HPO where multiple agents explore adjustment strategies concurrently. MedicalMLOmni achieves the best score on 19 of 20 benchmarks; PMC-VQA is the exception, where a vision-language model with broader pre-training leads. Backbone-matched controls attribute the gains to the framework, not the backbone. By removing coding requirements, MedicalMLOmni lowers the barrier for domain experts with rich datasets but limited engineering expertise.

[742] arXiv:2610.28411 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Brain2Vec: A Self-Supervised 3D Foundation Model for Structural Brain MRI
Spiros Maggioros, Guray Erus, Gareth Harman, George Aidinis, Alexander Getka, Aristeidis Sotiras, Christos Davatzikos
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Deep learning models have become essential tools in medical imaging, yet training them end-to-end for diverse tasks remains challenging due to limited labeled data and computational constraints. To address this, we introduce Brain2Vec, a foundation model pre-trained on 74,425 T1-weighted Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) scans pooled from multiple studies. Brain2Vec can serve both as a weight initialization backbone for fine-tuning downstream tasks and as a standalone feature extractor. We evaluated Brain2Vec in three tasks: downstream predictive performance, convergence speed, and embedding quality. Using Brain2Vec's pretrained weights as initialization and fine-tuning on labeled data for a brain age prediction task, results demonstrate improved final accuracy and faster convergence compared to random initialization. Additionally, its frozen embeddings outperform anatomically defined volumetric features on four of five downstream classification tasks and perform competitively with a state-of-the-art foundation model pre-trained on substantially more data. Lastly, we show that Brain2Vec encodes information primarily from a spatially localized and neuroanatomically meaningful set of brain regions, and that manipulating a subset of latent features produces monotonic, region-specific effects on the reconstructed anatomy. Brain2Vec code and trained models are available as an open-source package on this https URL. Users can apply Brain2Vec locally by installing the package, or directly through the NiChart cloud platform this https URL, where Brain2Vec features can be derived without requiring local installation or specialized infrastructure.

[743] arXiv:2610.28416 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Code2Video-Compass: A Comprehensive Benchmark for General-Purpose Code-Based Video Generation across T2V, I2V, and V2V
Zhenghan Chen, Zekai Shao, Xin Lin, Leting Cheng, Siming Chen
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Code-based video generation offers fine-grained control, targeted editing, and component reuse compared with direct video generation. This approach requires multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to translate visual and temporal requirements into executable programs that produce complete videos. However, existing code-based benchmarks primarily target specialized tasks, leaving complete video creation across diverse creative categories and input modalities insufficiently evaluated. We introduce Code2Video-Compass, a general-purpose benchmark for code-based video generation across text-to-video (T2V), image-to-video (I2V), and video-to-video (V2V) settings. Code2Video-Compass comprises 2,104 tasks spanning 10 categories, 24 subtypes, and three complexity dimensions covering construction, dynamic animation, and state dependency. It combines tasks curated from textual instructions and visual references with corresponding T2V, I2V, and V2V tasks derived from complete professional and user-created videos. We propose a dual-level evaluation framework combining 12 objective metrics and five subjective metrics. Objective evaluation covers operational performance, video quality, text-video alignment, and reference fidelity, while subjective evaluation uses an MLLM judge to evaluate instruction following and holistic video quality. Extensive evaluation of 15 recent proprietary and open-weight MLLMs from nine families reveals that even leading models face challenges in reliably generating high-quality complete videos aligned with textual and visual requirements, with performance generally declining as construction, dynamic animation, and state-dependency complexity increases. We anticipate that Code2Video-Compass will advance reliable, coherent, and controllable code-based video generation and inspire broader progress in programmatic visual creation.

[744] arXiv:2610.28419 [pdf, html, other]
Title: DISTRACT: Degradation-Indexed Study of Textual Reference Across Competing Targets
Dan Zlotnikov, Ohad Ben-Shahar
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Vision-language trackers (VLTs) accept descriptions intended to assist tracking, but accepting text does not establish that its content changes tracking decisions, particularly as visual evidence deteriorates. We introduce DISTRACT, a matched-intervention benchmark that holds video, target, and distractor fixed while crossing four text priors with four image degradations along a controlled severity axis. We evaluate five VLTs on four datasets using behavioral contrasts, layerwise representation probes, and activation patching. Molmo2 and JointNLT exhibit directed text use. Some effects contract under degradation, whereas others show no significant endpoint change after multiplicity correction. UVLTrack, MMTrack, and DUTrack respond only weakly to changes in text semantics, with no directed behavioral effect surviving FDR correction in the tested settings. Model-internal analyses reveal that at decision-near states, correct-versus-conflicting text is decodable in Molmo2 and JointNLT but not in the other three systems. In the responsive models, decodability peaks at late states where replacement produces little behavioral change, whereas replacing selected earlier states redirects conflict-associated trajectories toward the target. Because matched-correct donors do not significantly outperform unrelated donors, these interventions identify earlier intervention-sensitive states without establishing target-specific semantic rescue. DISTRACT thus exposes when and where text affects tracking under degraded visual evidence.

[745] arXiv:2610.28423 [pdf, html, other]
Title: WorldSR: Harnessing World Knowledge Search for Grounded Image Super-Resolution
Junyuan Deng, Xinyi Wu, Zhenyao Wu, Song Wang, Yu Wang, Congchao Zhu
Comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Project Page: this https URL
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Generative-prior-based super-resolution (SR) methods leverage implicit knowledge learned from large-scale models to enhance low-resolution inputs. However, such priors are inherently stochastic and optimized for diverse generation, conflicting with the deterministic, high-fidelity reconstruction required for SR. It is also tied to the base model, costly to update, and prone to hallucinations as real-world data evolves. To address these limitations, we introduce WorldSR, a novel framework that augments SR with explicit, entity-aligned visual world knowledge. WorldSR automatically decomposes the input into semantic entities and performs entity-wise retrieval of structurally and semantically aligned images from a large-scale external corpus. For efficiency and reliability, we incorporate a memory mechanism to reuse previously retrieved results and a multi-step filtering process to refine candidate references. The selected references as world knowledge are then integrated through a novel multi-reference super-resolution model, which provides fine-grained constraints for detail synthesis and structural recovery. Experiments on real-world SR benchmarks show that WorldSR consistently improves structural fidelity and visual quality, outperforming existing generative super-resolution methods. Our results suggest that entity-level grounding in external visual world knowledge provides a simple and effective complement to model-bound generative priors.

[746] arXiv:2610.28425 [pdf, html, other]
Title: After the Attacker Leaves: Benchmarking Carryover Attacks on LLM Agents
Zhiyue Xu, Xukai Wang, Zhiyuan Huang, Mingjie Zhan, Jian Zhao, Xu-Yao Zhang
Comments: Accepted by EMNLP 2026 Main Conference
Subjects: Cryptography and Security (cs.CR); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Modern LLM agents persist state across sessions via two channels: long-lived memory files silently prepended to the system prompt, and scheduled tasks waking the agent without user input. A one-time indirect prompt injection committed to either channel can re-fire across sessions long after the attacker leaves, threats we term carryover attacks. Existing prompt-injection benchmarks evaluate attacks only in the session where malicious content is first observed, leaving the gate governing when and how often a planted payload later re-fires unmeasured. We present CarryoverBench: 12 personal-assistant scenarios and 101 attack tasks across three trigger channels: Instant, same-turn IPI; Autonomous, heartbeat-scheduled; and Latent, memory-resurfaced. A rule-based verifier scores planting and triggering as independent stages. Across five frontier models, planted payloads re-fire without measurable decay over five rounds; conditional on successful planting, the trigger stage often provides little additional protection. Porting the Latent channel to a second runtime, Hermes, attenuates but does not eliminate the effect, suggesting that carryover defense requires runtime-layer controls in addition to prompt-level interventions.

[747] arXiv:2610.28427 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Region-Specific EEG Classification of Hypnotic Susceptibility Using a Sliding-Window 2D CNN: A Subject-Independent Evaluation
Krzysztof Wrobel, Grzegorz M. Wojcik
Comments: 8 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

We investigate whether a 2D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) trained on minimally preprocessed EEG signals can classify hypnotic susceptibility across distinct brain regions. Sixty-two male participants (32 Control, 30 Guided Imagery / Hipno group) underwent a 20-minute EEG recording using a 256-channel EGI cap. A sliding-window approach evaluates all 10-second windows within the recording for each of seven predefined brain regions (prefrontal, frontal, temporal, central, parietal, occipital, and facial), yielding up to 868 independently trained models. Initial screening with a segment-level 90/10 random split showed that five regions exceeded the 0.67 accuracy threshold, with the occipital region achieving the highest mean accuracy (0.721) across 90.3% of windows. Subject-independent evaluation via Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) cross-validation, however, substantially revised this picture: occipital performance collapsed to near-chance (mean ACC 0.453, AUC 0.429), revealing that high random-split accuracy was driven by subject-specific EEG fingerprints rather than genuine group differences. In contrast, the frontal and prefrontal regions maintained above-chance LOSO accuracy (0.646 and 0.624, respectively), demonstrating genuine generalisability. These results underscore the necessity of subject-independent validation in EEG-based classification studies and highlight anterior cortical regions as more reliable neural markers of hypnotic susceptibility.

[748] arXiv:2610.28429 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Racer: Hunting GPU Kernel Bugs with Symbolic Equivalence Checking
Tuan Truong Vu, Cheng Tan
Subjects: Symbolic Computation (cs.SC); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

GPU kernels are critical to the performance of today's AI services, yet the same operators are rewritten repeatedly: for each GPU generation, numeric format, serving regime, and kernel language. Every rewrite must preserve the function computed by the implementation it replaces. Today, this obligation depends almost entirely on differential testing: run the new kernel and a trusted reference on randomly sampled tensors, then compare their outputs within a tolerance. This approach has blind spots that additional test cases cannot eliminate. For example, a logical bug may produce an error smaller than the tolerance required to accommodate a correct optimized kernel.
We propose symbolic equivalence checking, which executes a kernel and its reference on symbolic inputs, turning each output cell into an exact algebraic expression, and then checks whether the paired expressions agree for all inputs. Because these expressions are exact, symbolic equivalence checking distinguishes floating-point error from logical bugs, while a single check covers the entire input space.
We implement Racer, a PTX-level symbolic equivalence checking engine, with three techniques that make this approach practical for production kernels: (1) Shape Reduction to control checking cost, (2) a lockstep CTA scheduler to handle concurrency, and (3) idiom templates with exact numeric refutation for otherwise inconclusive results. Across 2,408 production kernels from 41 collection targets, Racer found 82 real bugs in 23 libraries, including 76 previously unknown bugs and 41 confirmed so far.

[749] arXiv:2610.28430 [pdf, html, other]
Title: A Digital Twin to Improve Cyber-Social Impact
Vita Santa Barletta, Danilo Caivano, Gabriel Cellammare, Andrea Dimauro, Pasquale Mesagna, Massimiliano Morga
Comments: 16 pages, 5 figures
Journal-ref: SHIELD-AI co-located in European Conference on Machine Learning and Principles and Practice of Knowledge Discovery in Databases - ECML PKDD 2026
Subjects: Cryptography and Security (cs.CR); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

The increasing complexity of Industrial Control Systems (ICS) and their integration with IT infrastructures has significantly expanded the cyber threat landscape. Traditional cybersecurity models, primarily based on the Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability (CIA triad), fail to capture the broader societal and operational impacts of cyberattacks. This paper proposes a novel framework that integrates Digital Twin technology with a Cyber-Social Security model to simulate, analyze, and quantify cyber threats in critical infrastructures. Virtualized ICS environments built with Mininet and MiniCPS are used to model attack scenarios and assess their consequences across technical and social dimensions. At the core of the framework lies the Cyber-Social Vulnerability Scoring System (CSVSS), a quantitative metric that extends CVSS with a Social Impact dimension grounded in the Entity and Place pillars, producing a single, reproducible severity score that reflects real-world consequences. Crucially, the framework does not automate risk assessment but keeps the human analyst at its center: a Large Language Model (LLM) performs a first-pass analysis, mapping vulnerabilities and drafting risk reports, while the analyst, supported by explainable AI feedback, validates the findings and retains decision authority over critical cases. Experimental results demonstrate the framework's ability to model and score cyber-social impact, while the human-in-the-loop design is presented as a conceptual principle to preserve oversight.

[750] arXiv:2610.28431 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Plausible Future, Wrong Choice: Steering World-Action Models toward Intended Future
Zhuohao Li, Jiawei He, Yuxuan Yan, Lang Zhou, Yinghao Li, Yanrui Li, Tianyu Zhang, Yi-Yang Song, Xirui Wu andYi-Lin Wei, Fating Hong, Qing Zhang, Zhilin Zhao, Jingdong Wang, Wei-Shi Zheng
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

World-Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for embodied generalist policies by jointly modeling future world evolution and robot actions across diverse manipulation tasks. However, representing diverse futures is only the first step: a capable WAM must also generate futures that match the requirements of the current task and execution progress. In long-horizon manipulation where similar observation-action segments occur across different tasks and stages, existing approaches may generate locally plausible yet misdirected rollouts to drift toward wrong task stage, i.e., a phenomenon we term Stage Confusion. To address this problem, we propose TaskWAM, a closed-loop, stage-aware framework that represents fine-grained task requirements with Mode Tokens and tracks execution progress with State Tokens, forming a structured task state to steer world--action generation toward intended future. We further introduce StageBench, a controlled multi-stage manipulation benchmark with parameterized stage variations and automated this http URL experiments on both simulation benchmarks and real-world tasks demonstrate that TaskWAM effectively reduces confusion and achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods.
