Building on this, we propose an algorithm that solves the problem in $O(m^{1.5} \log^2 m)$ time and $O(m \log^2 m)$ space, where $m$ is the size of the RLE-compressed input string. Furthermore, we propose another algorithm for the problem that runs in average $O(m \log^2 m)$ time and $O(m\log m)$ space: The average-case bound holds under an exponent-bounded random-input model, in which the input is chosen uniformly from the strings of RLE size $m$ whose run exponents are at most a given bound $E\geq 2$. Our approaches extend key ideas from [Gawrychowski et al., SPIRE 2015] to the RLE setting through new combinatorial insights. When the RLE size $m$ is sufficiently small compared to $n$, our algorithms achieve linear-time behavior in $n$, potentially leading to improved performance over existing methods in such cases.

[981] arXiv:2507.21035 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: GenoMAS: Guided Multi-Agent Programming for Scientific Discovery from Genomic Data
Haoyang Liu, Yijiang Li, Haohan Wang
Comments: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 Findings. Project page at this https URL and code at this https URL
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Genomics (q-bio.GN)

Gene expression analysis holds the key to many biomedical discoveries, yet extracting insights from raw transcriptomic data remains challenging due to the complexity of multiple large, semi-structured files and the need for extensive domain expertise. Current approaches either rely on inflexible workflows that fail in edge cases or fully autonomous agents that lack the precision required for rigorous scientific inquiry. GenoMAS addresses this by presenting a team of LLM-based agents that integrates structured workflows with autonomous adaptability, orchestrating diverse specialized agents through typed message-passing protocols. At its core lies a guided-planning framework where programming agents decompose task guidelines into Action Units and dynamically choose to advance, revise, bypass, or backtrack, maintaining logical coherence while adapting to the idiosyncrasies of genomic data. On the GenoTEX benchmark, GenoMAS achieves 89.13% CSC for data preprocessing and 60.48% $F_1$ for identifying trait-associated genes, surpassing prior art by 10.61% and 16.85%. Beyond transcriptomics, it outperforms strong agent baselines on ScienceAgentBench and DiscoveryBench, two independent bioinformatics benchmarks. Qualitative analysis shows that GenoMAS identifies gene-phenotype associations that are biologically plausible and corroborated by the literature.

[982] arXiv:2507.21299 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Blending data and physics for reduced-order modeling of systems with spatiotemporal chaotic dynamics
Alex Guo, Michael D. Graham
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

While data-driven techniques are powerful tools for reduced-order modeling of systems with chaotic dynamics, great potential remains for leveraging known physics (i.e. a full-order model (FOM)) to improve predictive capability. We develop a hybrid reduced order model (ROM), informed by both data and FOM, for evolving spatiotemporal chaotic dynamics on an invariant manifold whose coordinates are found using an autoencoder. This approach projects the vector field of the FOM onto the invariant manifold; then, this physics-derived vector field is either corrected using dynamic data, or used as a Bayesian prior that is updated with data. In both cases, the neural ordinary differential equation approach is used. We consider simulated data from the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky and complex Ginzburg-Landau equations. Relative to the data-only approach, for scenarios of abundant data, scarce data, and even an incorrect FOM (i.e. erroneous parameter values), the hybrid approach yields substantially improved time-series predictions.

[983] arXiv:2507.21917 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: ArtSeek: Deep artwork understanding via multimodal in-context reasoning and late interaction retrieval
Nicola Fanelli, Gennaro Vessio, Giovanna Castellano
Comments: Accepted at WACV 2027. 28 pages (10 main + 18 supplementary)
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Analyzing digitized artworks requires both visual interpretation and deep artistic, contextual, and historical knowledge. We introduce ArtSeek, a multimodal framework for art analysis that combines multimodal large language models with retrieval-augmented generation. Unlike prior work, our pipeline relies only on image input, so it applies to artworks without links to Wikidata or Wikipedia, common in most digitized collections. ArtSeek integrates three components: a late-interaction multimodal retrieval module, a contrastive multitask network predicting artist, genre, style, media, and tags, and an agentic reasoning strategy enabled through in-context examples. Central to this approach is WikiFragments, a dataset of image-text fragments extracted from the entire English Wikipedia to support knowledge-grounded multimodal reasoning. Our multimodal query encoding raises retrieval NDCG@5 from 33.9 to 44.9 over encoding the full image-text query, and fixed-budget token pooling keeps late-interaction search practical over millions of fragments at under 7% of the cost of full multi-vector retrieval. ArtSeek sets a new state of the art in artwork attribute classification, with +8.4% F1 in style classification over GraphCLIP, and gains +7.1 BLEU@1 on ArtPedia captioning. On five knowledge-grounded question answering benchmarks graded by an LLM judge from a different model family, retrieval helps where the answer is documented in our index or lies inside the classifier's label space (+0.19 mean correctness on two of them) and is neutral where it is not; what separates the two regimes is how much of a benchmark our knowledge base covers. The gain transfers to two non-Qwen backbones (+0.22 to +0.28). A blind human study and a qualitative analysis of successes and failures corroborate this picture and expose where retrieval still misleads. Data and code: this https URL

[984] arXiv:2507.23421 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Dual-Mode Wireless Devices for Adaptive Pull and Push-Based Communication
Sara Cavallero, Fabio Saggese, Junya Shiraishi, Israel Leyva-Mayorga, Shashi Raj Pandey, Chiara Buratti, Petar Popovski
Comments: Accepted to IEEE Transactions on Communications
Subjects: Networking and Internet Architecture (cs.NI)

This paper introduces a dual-mode communication framework for wireless devices that integrates query-driven (pull) and event-driven (push) transmissions within a unified time-frame structure. Devices typically respond to information requests in pull mode, but if an anomaly is detected, they preempt the regular response to report the critical condition. Additionally, push-based communication is used to proactively send critical data without waiting for a request. This adaptive approach ensures timely, context-aware, and efficient data delivery across different network conditions. To achieve high energy efficiency, we incorporate a wake-up radio mechanism and we design a tailored medium access control (MAC) protocol that supports data traffic belonging to the different communication classes. A comprehensive system-level analysis is conducted, accounting for the wake-up control operation and evaluating three key performance metrics: the success probability of anomaly reports (push traffic), the success probability of query responses (pull traffic) and the total energy consumption. Numerical results characterize the system's behavior and highlight the inherent trade-off between push and pull success probabilities as a function of allocated communication resources. Our analysis demonstrates that the proposed approach achieves up to a 42% reduction in energy consumption per served packet compared to traditional approaches, while maintaining reliable support for both communication paradigms.

[985] arXiv:2508.01300 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: How Far Are LLMs from Symbolic Planners? An NLP-Based Perspective
Ma'ayan Armony, Albert Meroño-Peñuela, Gerard Canal
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

AI planning provides agents the ability to act autonomously towards achieving a goal in a given environment. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have introduced the prospect of using unstructured input for planning, making LLMs in planning an active area of research, especially for supporting autonomous agents. However, LLMs remain unreliable as long-horizon planners, since some of the plans they produce contain mistaken or hallucinated actions; executing such plans could lead to unexpected and harmful outcomes. Existing benchmarks for LLMs in planning primarily rely on binary evaluation metrics, providing limited insight into the quality of plans that do not achieve the goal, and how far those are from becoming valid. In this paper, we frame the evaluation of LLMs in planning as a natural language processing (NLP) task, as LLMs are themselves NLP models. We propose a pipeline comprising three NLP-based steps that assess plan quality from complementary perspectives, followed by a symbolic planning step to achieve a valid plan, to provide a finer-grained understanding of the quality of invalid plans. In our experiments, we find no clear evidence of logical derivation or state-tracking during LLM plan generation -- on average, for all non-empty plans, only 3.55 actions per plan are executable, despite symbolically-generated optimal plans having an average length of 9.47 actions, which suggests that LLMs are still far from the reliability of symbolic planners. Our suite of metrics is further used to investigate patterns in LLM plan generation over time, and can provide a useful metric for assessing the quality of individual invalid plans.

[986] arXiv:2508.04262 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: One-weight codes in the sum-rank metric
Usman Mushrraf, Ferdinando Zullo
Subjects: Information Theory (cs.IT); Combinatorics (math.CO)

One-weight codes, in which all nonzero codewords share the same weight, form a highly structured class of linear codes with deep connections to finite geometry. While their classification is well understood in the Hamming and rank metrics - being equivalent to (direct sums of) simplex codes - the sum-rank metric presents a far more intricate landscape. In this work, we explore the geometry of one-weight sum-rank metric codes, focusing on three distinct classes. First, we introduce and classify \emph{constant rank-list} sum-rank codes, where each nonzero codeword has the same tuple of ranks, extending results from the rank-metric setting. Next, we investigate the more general \emph{constant rank-profile} codes, where, up to reordering, each nonzero codeword has the same tuple of ranks. Although a complete classification remains elusive, we present the first examples and partial structural results for this class. Finally, we consider one-weight codes that are also MSRD (Maximum Sum-Rank Distance) codes. For dimension two, constructions arise from partitions of scattered linear sets on projective lines. For dimension three, we connect their existence to that of special $2$-fold blocking sets in the projective plane, leading to new bounds and nonexistence results over certain fields.

[987] arXiv:2508.11850 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: LLM-Guided Evolution of Symbolic Acceleration Inequality Families for MILP
Milad Yazdani, Mahdi Mostajabdaveh, Samin Aref, Zirui Zhou
Journal-ref: Transactions on Machine Learning Research (2026)
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Integer programming (IP) is central to many combinatorial optimization tasks but remains challenging due to its NP-hard nature. A practical way to improve IP solvers is to manually design inequality families that exploit problem structure. However, this creative process requires deep expertise and has therefore been difficult to automate. Our proposed framework, Symbolic Acceleration via Generative Evolution (SAGE), automates symbolic discovery of acceleration inequality families at the modeling level. It reasons over a symbolic IP formulation and a natural language description of the problem to discover a reusable set of acceleration inequality families that can be instantiated for each problem instance. These acceleration inequality families are selected through empirical admissibility and impact screening rather than mathematical proofs. SAGE (i) initializes a population of candidate acceleration inequality families via an initializer agent that uses an LLM; (ii) it screens candidates for admissibility on a small development admissibility set for solution feasibility and the separation of the relaxation solution; and (iii) it iteratively refines the population of inequalities through evolutionary crossover and mutation agents. Across seven MILP benchmarks, SAGE reduces optimality gaps by up to $62.1\%$ relative to baseline MILP formulations solved with a fixed time budget and reaches target gaps up to $5.51\times$ faster according to shifted geometric mean speedup. Comprehensive ablations show its robustness across different LLM backends and across solvers and internal cut settings. Code: this https URL

[988] arXiv:2508.20784 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Single Agent Robust Deep Reinforcement Learning for Bus Fleet Control
Yifan Zhang, Liang Zheng, Qifan Zhang
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Bus bunching remains a challenge for urban transit due to stochastic traffic and passenger demand. Traditional solutions rely on multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) in loop-line settings, which overlook realistic operations characterized by heterogeneous routes, timetables, fluctuating demand, and varying fleet sizes. We propose a novel single-agent reinforcement learning (RL) framework for bus holding control that avoids the data imbalance and convergence issues of MARL under near-realistic simulation. A bidirectional timetabled network with dynamic passenger demand is constructed. The key innovation is reformulating the multi-agent problem into a single-agent one by augmenting the state space with categorical identifiers (vehicle ID, station ID, time period) in addition to numerical features (headway, occupancy, velocity). This high-dimensional encoding enables single-agent policies to capture inter-agent dependencies, analogous to projecting non-separable inputs into a higher-dimensional space. We further design a structured reward function aligned with operational goals: instead of exponential penalties on headway deviations, a ridge-shaped reward balances uniform headways and schedule adherence. Experiments show that our modified soft actor-critic (SAC) achieves more stable and superior performance than benchmarks, including MADDPG (e.g., -430k vs. -530k under stochastic conditions). These results demonstrate that single-agent deep RL, when enhanced with categorical structuring and schedule-aware rewards, can effectively manage bus holding in non-loop, real-world contexts. This paradigm offers a robust, scalable alternative to MARL frameworks, particularly where agent-specific experiences are imbalanced.

[989] arXiv:2508.20976 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: WoW-Bench: Evaluating Fine-Grained Acoustic Perception in Audio-Language Models via Marine Mammal Vocalizations
Jaeyeon Kim, Heeseung Yun, Sang Hoon Woo, Chao-Han Huck Yang, Gunhee Kim
Comments: Findings of ACL 2026. Project page: this https URL
Journal-ref: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2026, pages 31208-31229
Subjects: Sound (cs.SD); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Audio and Speech Processing (eess.AS)

Large audio-language models (LALMs) extend language understanding into the auditory domain, yet their ability to perform low-level listening, such as pitch and duration detection, remains underexplored. However, low-level listening is critical for real-world, out-of-distribution tasks where models must reason about unfamiliar sounds based on fine-grained acoustic cues. To address this gap, we introduce the World-of-Whale benchmark (WoW-Bench) to evaluate low-level auditory perception and cognition using marine mammal vocalizations. We use marine mammal vocalizations as out-of-distribution sound events to better assess models' low-level listening and so that the models do not rely on prior knowledge of the sound events. WoW-bench is composed of a Perception benchmark for categorizing novel sounds and a Cognition benchmark, inspired by Bloom's taxonomy, to assess the abilities to remember, understand, apply, and analyze sound events. For the Cognition benchmark, we additionally introduce distractor questions to evaluate whether models are truly solving problems through listening rather than relying on other heuristics. Experiments with state-of-the-art LALMs show performance far below human levels, indicating a need for stronger auditory grounding in LALMs.

[990] arXiv:2509.00362 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Optimized Weight Initialization on the Stiefel Manifold for Deep ReLU Neural Networks
Hyungu Lee, Taehyeong Kim, Hayoung Choi
Comments: 18 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Stable and efficient training of ReLU networks with large depth is highly sensitive to weight initialization. Improper initialization can cause permanent neuron inactivation dying ReLU and exacerbate gradient instability as network depth increases. Methods such as He, Xavier, and orthogonal initialization preserve variance or promote approximate isometry. However, they do not necessarily regulate the pre-activation mean or control activation sparsity, and their effectiveness often diminishes in very deep architectures. This work introduces a semi-orthogonal initialization specifically optimized for ReLU by solving an optimization problem on the Stiefel manifold, thereby preserving scale and calibrating the pre-activation statistics from the outset. A family of closed-form solutions and an efficient sampling scheme are derived. Theoretical analysis at initialization shows that the proposed initialization mitigates dying ReLU, slows the decay of activation variance, and alleviates gradient vanishing, thereby stabilizing signal and gradient flow in deep architectures. Empirically, across MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, multiple tabular datasets, few-shot settings, and ReLU-family activations, the proposed initialization maintains stable performance as network depth increases, with particularly clear advantages in few-shot learning and large-depth settings.

[991] arXiv:2509.01231 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Unpacking "Personal" Health Informatics for Proactive Collective Care
Shyama Sastha Krishnamoorthy Srinivasan, Mohan Kumar, Pushpendra Singh
Comments: 29 pages, 5 figures, 6 tables; A qualitative HCI study with prototype evaluation; Preprint of paper accepted at PACM HCI (CSCW)
Subjects: Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC); Computers and Society (cs.CY)

Care is primarily a collective phenomenon, with a practice that involves sharing health and wellbeing information within a trusted "care circle" of family and companions for sensemaking, interpretation, decision-making, and follow-through. However, current digital health tools and systems are designed for individuals and primarily intended for Personal Health Informatics (PHI). This mismatch between collective practice and individualistic design creates new challenges for the proactive use of such systems in care settings and limits adoption, sustained engagement, and meaningful use. To examine how people practice collective care and how (if) they perceive, adopt, and integrate PHI systems for proactive care, we conducted a sequential mixed-methods study. Through an initial survey (n=87) and semi-structured interviews (n=22), we found that their practices involve collectively analyzing and sensemaking health information. However, we also found that their use of existing systems to support such practices is constrained by factors at personal, relational, technological, and structural levels that evolve over time. To address these constraints and explore redesigning PHI toward "Collective Health Informatics", we conducted eight stakeholder interviews (n=12), a follow-up survey (n=114), and six co-design workshops (n=12) to understand the dynamics required in collective settings while retaining agency. Using a design probe evaluation (n=38), we refine a design vision for coordinated, trustworthy action across such care relationships. Our findings motivate CC-Proact, an operational map that translates ecological influences into three design levers: Agency, Elicitation, and Engagement. Using this map, our work empirically examines collective care practices and offers six design recommendations to build responsible systems that proactively support collective care.

[992] arXiv:2509.04777 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Forall-Exists Relational Verification by Filtering to Forall-Forall
Ramana Nagasamudram, Anindya Banerjee, Jude Kanjamala, David A. Naumann
Comments: v2: expanded evaluation section; expository improvements throughout; v3: add missing author in metadata
Subjects: Logic in Computer Science (cs.LO); Programming Languages (cs.PL)

Relational verification encompasses reasoning about data abstraction, security and privacy, secure compilation, and functional specification of tensor programs, among others. Several relational logics and tools support compositional reasoning about $\forall\forall$ (2-safety) properties and, generally, $k$-safety properties. In contrast, few logics and tools exist for reasoning about $\forall\exists$ properties which are critical in the presence of nondeterminism. This paper's primary contribution is a technique for verifying a $\forall\exists$ judgment by way of a novel transformation. The filter-adequacy transformation adds assertions to a product program in such a way that the desired $\forall\exists$ property (of a pair of underlying unary programs) is implied by a $\forall\forall$ property of the transformed product. The paper develops bicoms, a form of product programs that facilitates expressing good alignments and caters for direct translation of $\forall\forall$ properties to unary correctness; proves that successful $\forall\forall$ verification of a transformed bicom implies the $\forall\exists$ spec for its underlying unary commands; and evaluates the technique using a prototype auto-active relational verifier. The technique enables users to work with ordinary assertions and assumptions, and a standard assertion language, so that existing $\forall\forall$ and unary verification tools can be used for $\forall\exists$.

[993] arXiv:2509.10562 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Predator-Prey Model: Driven Hunt for Accelerated Grokking
I. A. Lopatin, S. V. Kozyrev, A. N. Pechen
Comments: 18 pages, 9 figures, 3 tables
Journal-ref: IEEE Transactions on Artificial Intelligence, 7(10), 5753-5763, (2026)
Subjects: Neural and Evolutionary Computing (cs.NE); Adaptation and Self-Organizing Systems (nlin.AO)

A machine learning method is proposed using two agents (representing two coupled replicas of the model parameters) that simulate the biological behavior of a predator and a prey. In this method, the two agents interact with each other via a pair of potentials that simulate the dynamics when the predator chases the prey while the prey runs away from the predator - to perform an optimization on the landscape. This method allows, for optimization landscapes with narrow ravines with gentle slope or even flat bottoms, to avoid optimization getting stuck in a ravine. For some examples of grokking (i.e., delayed generalization) problems we show that this method allows for achieving up to a hundred times faster learning in gradient evaluations and up to 60 times in the wall-clock time compared to the standard learning procedure.

[994] arXiv:2509.13582 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Convergence of pivoted Cholesky for Lipschitz kernels
Sungwoo Jeong, Alex Townsend, Christopher Wang
Comments: 19 pages, 4 figures
Subjects: Numerical Analysis (math.NA)

We investigate the continuous analogue of the Cholesky factorization, namely the pivoted Cholesky algorithm. Our analysis establishes quantitative convergence guarantees for kernels of minimal smoothness. We prove that for a symmetric positive definite Lipschitz continuous kernel $K:\Omega\times \Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ on a compact domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^d$, the residual of the Cholesky algorithm with complete pivoting (where the maximum value of the diagonal of the residual is selected as the next pivot) is uniformly bounded above by a constant multiple of the separation distance of the pivots, which implies the convergence rate $\|R_n\|_\infty=\mathcal{O}(n^{-1/d})$, where $R_n$ is the residual after $n$ Cholesky steps and $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ is the supremum norm. Along the way, we show that for any pivoting strategy, $\|R_n\|_\infty$ is bounded by a constant multiple of the fill distance of the pivots. Moreover, if $K$ is differentiable in both variables with a Lipschitz derivative and $\Omega$ is convex, our convergence rate improves to $\mathcal{O}(n^{-2/d})$. Our result closes a gap between theory and practice as previous analyses required $K$ to be $C^2$-regular or translation invariant to establish convergence, whereas empirical evidence indicated robust performance even for non-differentiable kernels. We further prove a connection between the Cholesky algorithm and the P-greedy interpolation method, as well as downstream applications to Gaussian process regression and matrix Cholesky factorization.

[995] arXiv:2509.18912 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Frequency-Domain Decomposition and Recomposition for Robust Audio-Visual Segmentation
Kai Peng, Yunzhe Shen, Miao Zhang, Jia Wang, Leiye Liu, Wei Ji, Jingjing Li, Yongri Piao, Huchuan Lu
Comments: Accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Image Processing (TIP), 2026
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Audio-visual segmentation (AVS) plays a critical role in multimodal machine learning by effectively integrating audio and visual cues to precisely segment objects or regions within visual scenes. Recent AVS methods have demonstrated significant improvements. However, they overlook the inherent frequency-domain contradictions between audio and visual modalities--the substantial noise often present in audio high-frequency signals vs. the structurally rich details in visual high-frequency signals. Ignoring these differences can result in suboptimal performance. In this paper, we rethink the AVS task from a deeper perspective by reformulating AVS task as a frequency-domain decomposition and recomposition problem. To this end, we introduce a novel Frequency-Aware Audio-Visual Segmentation (FAVS) framework consisting of two key modules: Frequency-Domain Enhanced Decomposer (FDED) module and Synergistic Cross-Modal Consistency (SCMC) module. FDED module employs a residual-based iterative frequency decomposition to discriminate modality-specific semantics and structural features, and SCMC module leverages a mixture-of-experts architecture to reinforce semantic consistency and modality-specific feature preservation through dynamic expert routing. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our FAVS framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on three benchmark datasets, and abundant qualitative visualizations further verify the effectiveness of the proposed FDED and SCMC modules. The project repository is available at this https URL.

[996] arXiv:2509.22407 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: EMMA: Enhancing Robotic Control Robustness through a Generative Visual Model
Zhehao Dong, Xiaofeng Wang, Zheng Zhu, Yirui Wang, Yang Wang, Yukun Zhou, Boyuan Wang, Chaojun Ni, Runqi Ouyang, Wenkang Qin, Xinze Chen, Yun Ye, Guan Huang, Zhen Lu, Yue Yang
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Robotics (cs.RO)

The generalization of vision-language-action (VLA) models heavily relies on diverse training data. However, acquiring large-scale robot manipulation data across varied object appearances is costly and labor-intensive. To address this, we introduce Embodied Manipulation Media Adaptation (EMMA), a framework for augmenting VLA policies that combines a generative data engine with an effective training pipeline. We introduce DreamTransfer, a diffusion Transformer-based architecture for generating multi-view consistent and geometrically plausible embodied manipulation videos. It supports text-driven video editing on foreground, background and lighting while preserving 3D structure and geometric fidelity. We also utilize a hybrid training set of real and generated data and propose AdaMix to enhance the training process. AdaMix is a training strategy that adaptively weights samples according to policy performance to emphasize challenging samples. Evaluations show DreamTransfer outperforms previous video generation models in multi-view consistency, geometric fidelity, and text-conditioning precision. In real-world robotic tasks with zero-shot visual settings, our framework achieves a relative performance increase of over 92% compared to training with real data alone, and improves by an additional 17% with AdaMix.

[997] arXiv:2509.24608 (replaced) [pdf, other]
Title: Evaluating utility of clinical prediction models: A comparison of decision curve analysis and cost curves
Louise AC Millard, Matthew Sperrin, Richard M Martin, Peter A Flach
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Machine Learning (stat.ML)

Classification models typically predict a binary outcome and use one or more decision thresholds to produce a classification or inform a clinical decision. Decision curves and cost curves are model evaluation approaches that assess net benefit and loss across decision thresholds. In this paper we compare decision curves and cost curves, demonstrating that decision curves are closely related to a specific type of cost curve called a Brier curve. Users of both approaches set the classification threshold assuming calibrated model scores, using the relative clinical importance of correct positive and negative classifications. A given decision curve has a corresponding Brier curve such that reference lines common in each space can be included in either (e.g. the 'treat none' decision curve can be translated into an equivalent 'treat none' Brier curve). We suggest the upper envelope decision curve as a useful comparison to a model decision curve showing the maximum achievable net benefit through recalibration. We show that net benefit (used for decision curves) and Brier loss (used for Brier curves) will always choose the same model as optimal at any given threshold, but cannot be compared or aggregated across thresholds except under specific assumptions; doing so otherwise requires custom weightings.

[998] arXiv:2509.25921 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Achieving Pareto Optimality in Games via Single-bit Feedback
Seref Taha Kiremitci, Ahmed Said Donmez, Muhammed O. Sayin
Comments: Revised version of S. T. Kiremitci, A. S. Donmez, and M. O. Sayin, "Achieving Pareto Optimality in Games via Single-Bit Feedback," published in the Proceedings of ICASSP 2026. This revision expands the discussion of related work on decentralized welfare optimization with communication, adds references, and refines the description of our contributions
Subjects: Computer Science and Game Theory (cs.GT)

Efficient coordination in multi-agent systems often incurs high communication overhead or slow convergence rates, making scalable welfare optimization difficult. We propose Single-Bit Coordination Dynamics for Pareto-Efficient Outcomes (SBC-PE), a decentralized learning algorithm requiring only a single-bit satisfaction signal per agent each round. Despite this extreme efficiency, SBC-PE guarantees convergence to the exact optimal solution in arbitrary finite games. We establish explicit regret bounds, showing expected regret grows only logarithmically with the horizon, i.e., O(log T). Compared with prior payoff-based or bandit-style rules, SBC-PE uniquely combines minimal signaling, general applicability, and finite-time guarantees. These results show scalable welfare optimization is achievable under minimal communication constraints.

[999] arXiv:2510.03223 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Attention-Aligned Reasoning for Large Language Models
Hongxiang Zhang, Yuan Tian, Tianyi Zhang
Comments: EMNLP 2026 (Findings)
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Large Language Models (LLMs) tend to generate a long reasoning chain when solving complex tasks. However, as the reasoning chain extends, critical intermediate steps and the original prompt will be buried in the context, receiving insufficient attention and leading to errors. In this work, we present ATAR, a novel reasoning method that leverages the inherent reasoning structure to steer LLM attention. Our experiments show that ATAR outperforms SOTA methods across six benchmarks, achieving up to 15.39% absolute improvement. Furthermore, with ATAR, "non-reasoning" models achieve comparable or even better performance compared to reasoning models of the same size in most benchmarks. Finally, our ablation studies show that the attention alignment component contributes significantly, and that these improvements are persist under different attentionsteering backends.

[1000] arXiv:2510.03811 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Curriculum-Augmented GFlowNets For mRNA Sequence Generation
Aya Laajil, Abduragim Shtanchaev, Sajan Muhammad, Aya El Mir, Eric Moulines, Tiago Silva, Salem Lahlou
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Quantitative Methods (q-bio.QM)

We develop an approach for the de novo synthesis of messenger RNA (mRNA) sequences encoding target proteins. This requires optimizing multiple biological objectives over large combinatorial spaces defined by synonymous codon sequences, a setting where Reinforcement Learning (RL) methods suffer from mode collapse and Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) face sparse rewards over long horizons. To address these challenges, we propose Curriculum-Augmented GFlowNets (CAGFNs), a multi-objective GFlowNet trained with an adaptive length-based curriculum driven by learning progress. In a nutshell, CAGFNs learn from progressively harder tasks corresponding to longer target proteins. We evaluate CAGFNs on CodonDesignEnv, a novel codon-level environment that preserves protein identity via dynamic action masking. Our experiments show that CAGFNs achieve competitive or stronger Pareto-front coverage and diversity while converging up to 4 times faster than non-curriculum GFlowNets, and maintaining 100% sequence uniqueness compared to RL baselines.

[1001] arXiv:2510.04884 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Higher-Order Network Structure Inference: A Topological Approach to Network Selection
Adam Schroeder, Russell Funk, Jingyi Guan, Taylor Okonek, Lori Ziegelmeier
Subjects: Social and Information Networks (cs.SI)

Thresholding---the pruning of nodes or edges based on their properties or weights---is an essential preprocessing tool for extracting interpretable structure from complex network data, yet existing methods face several key limitations. Threshold selection often relies on heuristic methods or trial and error due to large parameter spaces and unclear optimization criteria, leading to sensitivity where small parameter variations produce significant changes in network structure. Moreover, most approaches focus on pairwise relationships between nodes, overlooking critical higher-order interactions involving three or more nodes. We introduce a systematic thresholding algorithm that uses topological data analysis to identify optimal network parameters by accounting for higher-order structural relationships. Our method uses persistent homology to favor thresholds at which the network's topological representation is stable under small parameter changes, subject to minimum requirements for higher-order features. Hyperparameters allow users to specify minimum requirements for topological features, effectively constraining the parameter search to avoid spurious solutions. We demonstrate the approach using networks of concepts linked by co-occurrence in scientific abstracts. Across scientific fields, paired comparisons with ten alternative thresholds favor our method at the median for finite-feature density and normalized total persistence in homological dimensions one and two. Our approach allows researchers to incorporate domain-specific constraints and extends beyond network thresholding to general parameterization problems in data analysis.

[1002] arXiv:2510.07073 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: VRPAgent: LLM-Driven Discovery of Heuristic Operators for Vehicle Routing Problems
André Hottung, Federico Berto, Chuanbo Hua, Nayeli Gast Zepeda, Daniel Wetzel, Michael Römer, Haoran Ye, Davide Zago, Michael Poli, Stefano Massaroli, Jinkyoo Park, Kevin Tierney
Comments: Published in TMLR
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Designing high-performing heuristics for vehicle routing problems (VRPs) is a complex task that requires both intuition and deep domain knowledge. Large language model (LLM)-based code generation has recently shown promise across many domains, but it still falls short of producing heuristics that rival those crafted by human experts. In this paper, we propose VRPAgent, a framework for VRPs that integrates LLM-generated components into a metaheuristic and refines them through a novel genetic search. By using the LLM to generate problem-specific operators, embedded within a shared metaheuristic framework for VRPs, VRPAgent keeps tasks manageable, guarantees correctness, and still enables the discovery of novel and powerful strategies. Across multiple VRPs, including the capacitated VRP, the VRP with time windows, and the prize-collecting VRP, our method discovers heuristic operators that outperform handcrafted methods and recent learning-based approaches while requiring only a single CPU core. To our knowledge, VRPAgent is one of the first LLM-based methods to advance the state-of-the-art in VRPs, highlighting a promising future for automated heuristics discovery.

[1003] arXiv:2510.10000 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Wasserstein Robust Classification Error: Surrogate Loss Misalignment and Distributional Attacks
Bach C. Le, Tung V. Dao, Binh T. Nguyen, Hong T.M. Chu
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Optimization and Control (math.OC); Machine Learning (stat.ML)

Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization (WDRO) provides a framework for evaluating model robustness through the worst-case expectation in the Wasserstein ball around a reference distribution. We prove that ordering hypotheses by increasing WDRO risk is equivalent to ordering them by decreasing robust accuracy if and only if the loss function is a positive multiple of the zero-one loss plus a label-dependent offset. For a class of loss functions including cross-entropy, we show that a hypothesis with perfect robust accuracy can conversely have a higher WDRO risk than another hypothesis with near zero robust accuracy. To evaluate robust accuracy directly, we develop Wasserstein distributional attacks (WDA), which add a weight generation stage after candidate support search to optimize the allocation of empirical mass under the Wasserstein constraint, rather than assigning each data point's full mass to one returned attack point as existing methods do. We further introduce a support-search algorithm for WDA that finds nearby misclassified inputs. On CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet, WDA using our search algorithm achieves the lowest adversarial accuracy in most tested settings. Our code is available at this https URL.

[1004] arXiv:2510.14697 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Mitigating Model Merging Conflicts via Knowledge-Aware Task Vector Purification
Bang An, Yibo Yang, Philip Torr, Bernard Ghanem
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Model merging aims to integrate task-specific abilities from individually fine-tuned models into a single model without extra training. In recent model merging methods, task vector has become a fundamental building block, as it can encapsulate the residual information from finetuning. However, the merged model often suffers from notable performance degradation due to the conflicts caused by task-irrelevant redundancy in task vectors. Existing efforts in overcoming redundancy by randomly dropping elements in the parameter space involves randomness and lacks knowledge awareness. To address these challenges, in this study, we propose Purifying TAsk Vectors (PAVE) in knowledge-aware subspace. Concretely, we sample some training examples from each task, and feed them into their corresponding fine-tuned models to acquire the covariance matrices before linear layers. We then perform a context-oriented singular value decomposition, which accentuates the weight components most relevant to the target knowledge. As a result, we can split fine-tuned model weights into task-relevant and redundant components in the knowledge-aware subspace, and purify the task vector by pruning the redundant components. To induce fair pruning efforts across models, we further introduce a spectral rank allocation strategy by optimizing a normalized activated pruning error. The task vector purification by our method as a plug-and-play scheme is applicable across various task vector-based merging methods to improve their performance. In experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of PAVE across a diverse set of merging methods, tasks, and model architectures.

[1005] arXiv:2510.23463 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Differential Privacy as a Perk: Federated Learning over Multiple-Access Fading Channels with a Multi-Antenna Base Station
Hao Liang, Haifeng Wen, Kaishun Wu, Khaled B. Letaief, Hong Xing
Comments: 20 pages, 8 figures, accpeted for IEEE J. Sel. Areas Commun
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Cryptography and Security (cs.CR); Machine Learning (stat.ML)

Federated Learning (FL) is a distributed learning paradigm that preserves privacy by eliminating the need to exchange raw data during training. In its prototypical edge instantiation with underlying wireless transmissions enabled by analog over-the-air computing (AirComp), referred to as \emph{over-the-air FL (AirFL)}, the inherent channel noise plays a unique role of \emph{frenemy} in the sense that it degrades training due to noisy global aggregation while providing a natural source of randomness for privacy-preserving mechanisms, formally quantified by \emph{differential privacy (DP)}. It remains, nevertheless, challenging to effectively harness such channel impairments, as prior arts, under assumptions of either simple channel models or restricted types of loss functions, mostly considering (local) DP enhancement with a single-round or non-convergent bound on privacy loss. In this paper, we study AirFL over multiple-access fading channels with a multi-antenna base station (BS) subject to user-level DP requirements. Despite a recent study, which claimed in similar settings that artificial noise (AN) must be injected to ensure DP in general, we demonstrate, on the contrary, that DP can be gained as a \emph{perk} even \emph{without} employing any AN. Specifically, we derive a novel bound on DP that converges under general bounded-domain assumptions on model parameters, along with a convergence bound with general smooth and non-convex loss functions. Next, we optimize over receive beamforming and power allocations to characterize the optimal convergence-privacy trade-offs, which also reveal explicit conditions in which DP is achievable without compromising training. Finally, our theoretical findings are validated by extensive numerical results.

[1006] arXiv:2510.26266 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: A Likely Geometry of Generative Models
Frederik Möbius Rygaard, Shen Zhu, Yinzhu Jin, Søren Hauberg, Tom Fletcher
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

The geometry of generative models serves as the basis for interpolation, model inspection, and more. Unfortunately, most generative models lack a principal notion of geometry without restrictive assumptions on either the model or the data dimension. In this paper, we construct a general geometry compatible with different metrics and probability distributions to analyze generative models that do not require additional training. We consider curves analogous to geodesics constrained to a suitable data distribution aimed at targeting high-density regions learned by generative models. We formulate this as a (pseudo)-metric and prove that this corresponds to a Newtonian system on a Riemannian manifold. We show that shortest paths in our framework can be characterized by a system of ordinary differential equations, which locally corresponds to geodesics under a suitable Riemannian metric. Numerically, we derive a novel algorithm to efficiently compute shortest paths and generalized Fréchet means. Quantitatively, we show that curves using our metric traverse regions of higher density than baselines across a range of models and datasets.

[1007] arXiv:2511.01553 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Online Continual Learning on Intel Loihi 2 via a Co-designed Spiking Neural Network
Elvin Hajizada, Danielle Rager, Timothy Shea, Leobardo Campos-Macias, Andreas Wild, Eyke Hüllermeier, Yulia Sandamirskaya, Mike Davies
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Neural and Evolutionary Computing (cs.NE)

Edge AI must adapt to new classes and shifting data within a tight power budget, but online continual learning (learning from each sample before the next arrives) is where conventional processors are least efficient: each small update pays a full dispatch at full power. We present CLP-SNN, a spiking architecture that recasts the Continually Learning Prototypes (CLP) algorithm as event-driven neural dynamics: a self-normalizing local rule replaces CLP's global renormalization, prototype allocation becomes novelty-triggered neurogenesis, and correctness-modulated plasticity becomes reward-gated per-neuron metaplasticity. Deployed on Intel Loihi 2 as the first online continual learner on that chip, rehearsal-free CLP-SNN matches Replay and SLDA on OpenLORIS at 1-shot; at 25-shot, it stays within 0.8 percentage points of Replay and 6.2 points below covariance-based SLDA. Each prediction-and-update step on extracted features completes on-chip in 0.33 ms at 0.05 mJ, 7.3x lower latency and 341x lower energy than Replay on a Jetson Orin Nano.

[1008] arXiv:2511.03345 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Improved Online Load Balancing in the Two-Norm
Sander Borst, Danish Kashaev
Comments: To appear in SODA 2027
Subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS)

We study the online load balancing problem on unrelated machines, with the objective of minimizing the square of the $\ell_2$ norm of the loads on the machines. The greedy algorithm of Awerbuch et al. (STOC'95) is optimal for deterministic algorithms and achieves a competitive ratio of $3 + 2 \sqrt{2} \approx 5.828$, and an improved $5$-competitive randomized algorithm based on independent rounding has been shown by Caragiannis (SODA'08). In this work, we present the first algorithm breaking the barrier of $5$ on the competitive ratio, achieving a bound of $5-c$ for some $c \geq 0.0157$. To obtain this result, we use a new primal-dual framework to analyze this problem based on a natural semidefinite programming relaxation, together with an online implementation of a correlated randomized rounding procedure of Im and Shadloo (SODA'20). This novel primal-dual framework also yields new, simple and unified proofs of the competitive ratio of the $(3 + 2 \sqrt{2})$-competitive greedy algorithm, the $5$-competitive randomized independent rounding algorithm, and that of a new $4$-competitive optimal fractional algorithm. We also provide lower bounds showing that the previous best randomized algorithm is optimal among independent rounding algorithms, that our new fractional algorithm is optimal, and that a simple greedy algorithm is optimal for the closely related online scheduling problem $R || \sum w_j C_j$.

[1009] arXiv:2511.14102 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Specter: Fast MoE Inference via Quantization-Enabled Multi-Step Speculative Offloading
Wenfeng Wang, Xiaofeng Hou, Xinfeng Xia, Xinkai WAng, Mingxuan Zhang, Peng Tang, Jiacheng Liu, Chao Li
Comments: Accepted to ASPLOS 2027. Includes the artifact appendix
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)

Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models often exceed a single accelerator's memory capacity. Offloading experts to host memory creates a severe PCIe I/O bottleneck because data-dependent routing keeps transfers on the critical path. We present Specter, an inference system that uses quantization to combine speculative decoding with expert offloading. Its lightweight quantized draft model runs efficiently on device while preserving high-fidelity expert activation patterns. This provides accurate multi-step lookahead over future expert usage, allowing the runtime to organize expert movement and execution ahead of verification and improve both communication and execution efficiency. Under single-request inference, Specter achieves an average 1.50x (up to 1.88x) speedup in time per output token (TPOT) over the state-of-the-art system. Specter makes memory-constrained, single-GPU MoE inference more practical on commodity hardware. Our code is available at this https URL.

[1010] arXiv:2511.15633 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Hierarchical Semantic Tree Anchoring for CLIP-Based Class-Incremental Learning
Tao Hu, Lan Li, Zhen-Hao Xie, Da-Wei Zhou
Comments: Accepted to NeurlPS 2026. Code is available at this https URL
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Class-Incremental Learning (CIL) enables models to learn new classes continually while preserving past knowledge. Recently, vision-language models like CLIP offer transferable features via multimodal pre-training, making them well-suited for CIL. However, real-world visual and linguistic concepts are inherently hierarchical: a textual concept like "dog" subsumes fine-grained categories such as "Labrador" and "Golden Retriever," and each category is associated with corresponding images. Nevertheless, existing CLIP-based CIL methods fail to explicitly capture this inherent hierarchy, leading to feature drift of fine-grained classes during incremental updates and ultimately to catastrophic forgetting. To address this challenge, we propose HASTEN (Hierarchical Semantic Tree Anchoring), a hierarchy-aware framework that uses semantic structure to stabilize CLIP-based CIL. Rather than treating classes as isolated labels, HASTEN leverages external hierarchical knowledge as structured supervision to organize visual and textual features in hyperbolic space, helping maintain parent--child relations as new tasks arrive and mitigating feature drift. Since the shared hyperbolic mapper is updated across tasks, we further stabilize it by constraining its updates to a null space induced by prior-task features, reducing interference with previous mappings while retaining adaptability to new classes. Extensive experiments on nine benchmarks show that HASTEN consistently outperforms existing methods while reducing feature drift and catastrophic forgetting. Code is available at: this https URL.

[1011] arXiv:2511.16084 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: SpectralTrain: A Universal Framework for Hyperspectral Image Classification
Meihua Zhou, Liping Yu, Xinyu Tong, Wai Kin Fung, Ruiguo Hu, Jiarui Zhao, Nan Wan
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Hyperspectral image (HSI) classification typically involves large-scale data and computationally intensive training, which limits the practical deployment of deep learning models in real-world remote sensing tasks. This study introduces SpectralTrain, a universal, architecture-agnostic training framework that enhances learning efficiency by integrating curriculum learning (CL) with principal component analysis (PCA)-based spectral downsampling. By gradually introducing spectral complexity while preserving essential information, SpectralTrain enables efficient learning of spectral -- spatial patterns at significantly reduced computational costs. The framework is independent of specific architectures, optimizers, or loss functions and is compatible with both classical and state-of-the-art (SOTA) models. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets -- Indian Pines, Salinas-A, and the newly introduced CloudPatch-7 -- demonstrate strong generalization across spatial scales, spectral characteristics, and application domains. The results indicate consistent reductions in training time by 2-7x speedups with small-to-moderate accuracy deltas depending on backbone. Its application to cloud classification further reveals potential in climate-related remote sensing, emphasizing training strategy optimization as an effective complement to architectural design in HSI models. Code is available at this https URL.

[1012] arXiv:2511.18354 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: From Crawled to Published: A Publisher-Controlled Web Architecture for an AI-Native Internet
Yixi Chen, Muhammad Bilal, Tie Ma, Zafar Ayyub Qazi, Marco Canini, Suhaib Fahmy
Subjects: Networking and Internet Architecture (cs.NI); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Information Retrieval (cs.IR)

AI agents, not humans, are becoming the web's primary consumers, yet the web still ships content structured for human browsing, with no native way for publishers to expose the semantic units within it. Access is therefore mediated by a handful of AI providers that crawl, chunk, and index content unilaterally, leaving publishers little control over how their content is represented, retrieved, or attributed. We argue this is a structural problem, not one better chunking or retrieval algorithms can solve. The web lacks a native layer for publisher-controlled semantic discovery and retrieval. We propose AISTRAL, an AI-Native Internet architecture that supplies this layer. Publishers expose semantically meaningful units (e.g., passages, claims, tables) through explicit, policy-governed interfaces they control, and a web-native semantic resolver, analogous to DNS but operating over meaning rather than location, lets agents discover relevant sources before retrieving fine-grained content directly from publishers. Our end-to-end prototype matches or exceeds representative centralized retrieval pipelines in answer quality, with up to 4.2x higher accuracy on large, specialized document collections. Against a public web-search agent, it answers up to 4.2x more questions correctly, while moving 2.9-41x less data per query. Because retrieval terminates at publisher-operated servers, attribution, provenance, and usage policies travel with the content, realigning incentives across the web ecosystem.

[1013] arXiv:2512.08365 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Magneton: Optimizing Energy Efficiency of ML Systems via Differential Energy Debugging
Yi Pan, Wenbo Qian, Dedong Xie, Ruiyan Hu, Yigong Hu, Baris Kasikci
Comments: 15 pages, 10 figures, to appear in the 24th USENIX Symposium on Networked Systems Design and Implementation (NSDI '27)
Subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

The training and deployment of machine learning (ML) models have become extremely energy-intensive. While existing optimization efforts focus primarily on hardware energy efficiency, a significant but overlooked source of inefficiency is software energy waste caused by poor software design. This often includes redundant or poorly designed operations that consume more energy without improving performance. These inefficiencies arise in widely used ML frameworks and applications, yet developers often lack the visibility and tools to detect and diagnose them.
We propose differential energy debugging, a novel approach that leverages the observation that competing ML systems often implement similar functionality with vastly different energy consumption. Building on this insight, we design and implement Magneton, an energy profiler that compares energy consumption between similar ML systems at the operator level and automatically pinpoints code regions and configuration choices responsible for excessive energy use. Applied to 9 popular ML systems spanning LLM inference, general ML frameworks, and image generation, Magneton detects and diagnoses 16 known cases of software energy inefficiency and further discovers 8 previously unknown cases, 7 of which have been confirmed by developers.

[1014] arXiv:2512.08814 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Ask, Answer, and Detect: Role-Playing LLMs for Personality Detection with Question-Conditioned Mixture-of-Experts
Yifan Lyu, Liang Zhang
Comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Main Conference, Poster)
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Understanding human personality is important for personalized recommendation and mental health assessment. Existing personality detection methods typically encode social media posts into user representations and predict personality labels. Despite advances in large language models (LLMs), these methods face limited supervision from scarce labels and an unclear mapping between user language and psychological constructs. We propose ROME, a framework that incorporates psychological knowledge into personality detection. Inspired by standardized self-assessment tests, ROME uses LLM role-playing to simulate users' responses to validated psychometric questionnaires. These question-level answers provide interpretable, questionnaire-grounded evidence and intermediate supervision. A question-conditioned Mixture-of-Experts module jointly routes post and question representations to predict questionnaire answers under explicit supervision. The predicted answers are aggregated into an interpretable answer vector and fused with user representations for final personality prediction in a multi-task learning framework. Experiments on two real-world datasets show that ROME outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, with relative improvements of 13.60% on Kaggle and 19.72% on Pandora. Code is available at this https URL.

[1015] arXiv:2512.08941 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: An Interactive Framework for Personalised Urban Accessibility Assessment
Prabhanjana Ghuriki, S. Chanti
Comments: 34 pages, 6 figures
Journal-ref: Discover Cities, 3(1), Article 204 (2026)
Subjects: Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC); Computers and Society (cs.CY)

Publicly available walkability tools are easy to use but place-based: they assign the same value to everyone sharing a location, computed from fixed category weights and category definitions calibrated on North American service landscapes. Accessibility research has long held that accessibility varies among individuals at the same location, and has accordingly developed preference- and person-sensitive measures; those measures are run as analyst-operated geographic information system workflows, out of reach of the residents whose preferences they represent. We present a deployed framework in which the preference structure is supplied by the user at query time. A user states which amenity categories matter, how much each matters, which are non-negotiable, which to avoid, which substitute for one another, and how far they will walk for each, and the map updates accordingly. This is possible because a rectangular travel impedance reduces the measure to the number of amenities reachable within a user-set threshold, which can be precomputed via shortest-path routing, leaving only arithmetic at query time. The score also stays interpretable: it is bounded, and each category's contribution can be read on its own. We evaluate the framework across Bengaluru, reporting its sensitivity to discretisation choices and comparing it against existing measures using identical inputs. Configuration moves ward rankings considerably more than the choice of aggregation does.

[1016] arXiv:2512.09365 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: KGOT: Unified Knowledge Graph and Optimal Transport Pseudo-Labeling for Molecule-Protein Interaction Prediction
Jiayu Qin, Zhengquan Luo, Guy Tadmor, Changyou Chen, David Zeevi, Zhiqiang Xu
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Predicting molecule-protein interactions (MPIs) is a fundamental task in computational biology, with crucial applications in drug discovery and molecular function annotation. However, existing MPI models face two major challenges. First, the scarcity of labeled molecule-protein pairs significantly limits model performance, as available datasets capture only a small fraction of biological relevant interactions. Second, most methods rely solely on molecular and protein features, ignoring broader biological context such as genes, metabolic pathways, and functional annotations that could provide essential complementary information. To address these limitations, our framework first aggregates diverse biological datasets, including molecular, protein, genes and pathway-level interactions, and then develop an optimal transport-based approach to generate high-quality pseudo-labels for unlabeled molecule-protein pairs, leveraging the underlying distribution of known interactions to guide label assignment. By treating pseudo-labeling as a mechanism for bridging disparate biological modalities, our approach enables the effective use of heterogeneous data to enhance MPI prediction. We evaluate our framework on multiple MPI datasets including virtual screening tasks and protein retrieval tasks, demonstrating substantial improvements over state-of-the-art methods in prediction accuracies and zero shot ability across unseen interactions. Beyond MPI prediction, our approach provides a new paradigm for leveraging diverse biological data sources to tackle problems traditionally constrained by single- or bi-modal learning, paving the way for future advances in computational biology and drug discovery.

[1017] arXiv:2512.09496 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: When does Subgroup Balance Matter? Predicting Performance Sensitivity from Latent Separability
Anissa Alloula, Charles Jones, Zuzanna Wakefield-Skorniewska, Francesco Quinzan, Bartłomiej Papież
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Unequal representation of demographic groups in training data poses challenges to model generalisation across populations. Standard practice assumes that balancing subgroup representation always optimises performance. However, recent empirical results contradict this assumption: in some cases, imbalanced data distributions actually improve subgroup performance, and in others, subgroup performance is unaffected by the absence of an entire subgroup during training. We propose the latent separation hypothesis, which states that a fine-tuned model's dependence on subgroup representation is determined by the degree of separation between subgroups in the latent space of the pre-trained model. We formalise this hypothesis, provide theoretical analysis, validate it empirically across four vision and language datasets, and present preliminary evidence of a causal role through regularisation experiments. Finally, we show how quantitative analysis of latent subgroup separation can inform practical data collection and balancing decisions when fine-tuning foundation models.

[1018] arXiv:2512.11988 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: CARI4D: Category Agnostic 4D Reconstruction of Human-Object Interaction
Xianghui Xie, Bowen Wen, Yan Chang, Hesam Rabeti, Jiefeng Li, Ye Yuan, Gerard Pons-Moll, Stan Birchfield
Comments: Update table 1 and table 2 after fixing a bug in evaluation
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Accurate capture of human-object interaction from ubiquitous sensors like RGB cameras is important for applications in human understanding, gaming, and robot learning. However, inferring 4D interactions from a single RGB view is highly challenging due to the unknown object and human information, depth ambiguity, occlusion, and complex motion, which hinder consistent 3D and temporal reconstruction. Previous methods simplify the setup by assuming ground truth object template or constraining to a limited set of object categories. We present CARI4D, the first category-agnostic method that reconstructs spatially and temporarily consistent 4D human-object interaction at metric scale from monocular RGB videos. To this end, we propose a pose hypothesis selection algorithm that robustly integrates the individual predictions from foundation models, jointly refine them through a learned render-and-compare paradigm to ensure spatial, temporal and pixel alignment, and finally reasoning about intricate contacts for further refinement satisfying physical constraints. Experiments show that our method outperforms prior art by 38% on in-distribution dataset and 36% on unseen dataset in terms of reconstruction error. Our model generalizes beyond the training categories and thus can be applied zero-shot to in-the-wild internet videos. Our code and pretrained models will be publicly released.

[1019] arXiv:2512.13886 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: OPTIMA: Optimal One-shot Pruning for LLMs via Quadratic Programming Reconstruction
Mohammad Mozaffari, Samuel Kushnir, Maryam Mehri Dehnavi, Amir Yazdanbakhsh
Comments: Accepted at ACML 2026 (PMLR 353). 32 pages
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Performance (cs.PF)

Post-training pruning cuts the inference cost of large language models, yet it faces a trade-off: simple heuristics that zero weights are fast but degrade accuracy, while principled joint optimization methods recover accuracy but are computationally infeasible at modern scale. One-shot methods such as SparseGPT sit in between and apply efficient but approximate weight updates. To close this gap, we introduce OPTIMA, a practical one-shot post-training pruning method that balances accuracy and scalability. OPTIMA casts layer-wise weight reconstruction after mask selection as independent, column-wise quadratic programs (QPs) that share one Hessian per weight matrix. Solving these QPs yields, at solver convergence, the per-column minimizer of the layer-wise reconstruction objective under the shared Hessian, and the shared Hessian makes the QPs easy to batch on accelerators. We implement an accelerator-friendly QP solver that accumulates one Hessian per weight matrix and solves many small QPs in parallel with a convergence certificate per column, enabling one-shot post-training pruning at scale on a single accelerator without fine-tuning. OPTIMA integrates with existing mask selectors and improves average zero-shot accuracy in 40 of 49 (model, mask selector, sparsity) settings across the LLaMA and Gemma families, with mean gains of +0.61, +0.56, and +1.01 points at 50% unstructured, 2:4, and 60% unstructured sparsity, and up to +3.97 points at 60% sparsity, while matching ADMM-based exact reconstruction on its own masks. On an NVIDIA H100, OPTIMA prunes an 8B-parameter transformer end-to-end in 40 hours and 60 GB of peak GPU memory. This shows that principled column-wise QP reconstruction is a practical alternative to heuristic weight updates in one-shot post-training pruning.

[1020] arXiv:2512.17284 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Continuation-Adjusted Full-Support Indifference in a Feedback Stackelberg Attacker--Defender Attrition Game
Azhar Iqbal, James M. Chappell, Derek Abbott
Comments: 18 pages, one figure
Subjects: Computer Science and Game Theory (cs.GT)

Successful attacks that remove assets break two familiar static regularities: coverage need not deter attack, and the defender need not push coverage until its budget or an individual target saturates. We analyse a finite-horizon attacker--defender attrition game under a stagewise feedback-recommitment strong Stackelberg equilibrium. Our central result is a continuation adjustment that converts each state--period node into a static security game with shifted payoffs. At feasible full-support nodes, coverage remains indexed by one scalar attacker value, so backward induction uses scalar interval and endpoint calculations; boundary-support nodes require conditional linear programmes. Continuation losses can reverse an attacker's coverage swing, making a covered asset more attractive because it survives for later attacks. A three-asset, two-period instance is solved globally for every discount factor. It exhibits an exact singular threshold at which the optimal set expands, the selected policy jumps, and the defender abandons a previously protected asset and leaves budget unused with no target saturated, although both players' values remain continuous.

[1021] arXiv:2512.22428 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Robust Residual Correction via Selective Deployment for Time Series Forecasting
Jianxiang Xie, Yuncheng Hua, Mingyue Cheng, Flora D. Salim, Hao Xue
Comments: 18 pages. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Revised title, experimental analyses, and theoretical discussion
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Machine Learning (stat.ML)

Post-hoc residual correction can reduce forecasting error, but always-on updates often fail to generalize: when residual signals are weak or noisy, expressive correctors can overfit and even increase the overall forecasting errors. We introduce CRC, a robust residual correction framework that couples a hybrid corrector with a validation-calibrated selective deployment rule. CRC proposes corrections via a conservative ridge "floor" plus conditional nonlinear refinement, but deploys them only when held-out evidence indicates net error reduction over a frozen baseline forecaster. CRC treats when to revise a forecast as a validation-calibrated deployment decision, not only how to fit residuals. Across standard long-sequence benchmarks and multiple backbones, CRC improves horizon-averaged MSE and MAE in most dataset-backbone pairs, with particularly large gains on complex datasets (e.g., over 20% relative MSE reduction on Traffic). We additionally report the non-degradation rate (NDR) as a stability diagnostic of harmful updates and ablate the validation-calibrated "firewall" that stabilizes MSE gains.

[1022] arXiv:2512.23067 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: The Reward Model Selection Crisis in Personalized Alignment
Fady Rezk, Yuangang Pan, Chuan-Sheng Foo, Xun Xu, Nancy Chen, Henry Gouk, Timothy Hospedales
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Personalized alignment from preference data has focused primarily on improving personal reward model (RM) accuracy, with the implicit assumption that better preference ranking translates to better personalized behavior. However, in deployment, computational constraints necessitate inference-time adaptation such as reward-guided decoding (RGD) rather than per-user policy fine-tuning. This creates a critical but overlooked requirement: reward models must not only rank preferences accurately but also effectively guide generation. We demonstrate that standard RM accuracy fails catastrophically as a selection criterion for deployment-ready personalized rewards. We introduce policy accuracy; a metric quantifying whether RGD-adapted LLMs correctly discriminate between preferred and dispreferred responses and show that upstream RM accuracy correlates only weakly with downstream policy accuracy (Kendall's tau = 0.08--0.31). More critically, we introduce Pref-LaMP the first personalized alignment benchmark with ground-truth user completions, enabling direct behavioural evaluation. On Pref-LaMP, we expose a complete decoupling between discriminative ranking and generation metrics: methods with 20-point RM accuracy differences produce almost identical output quality, and methods with high ranking accuracy can fail to generate behaviorally aligned responses. These findings reveal that the field has been optimizing for proxy metrics that do not predict deployment performance, and that current personalized alignment methods fail to operationalize preferences into behavioral adaptation under realistic deployment constraints. In contrast, we find simple in-context learning (ICL) to be highly effective - dominating all reward-guided methods for models $\geq$3B parameters, achieving $\sim$3 point ROUGE-1 gains over the best reward method at 7B scale.

[1023] arXiv:2512.23136 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: When Language Learners Code-Switch: Korean-English Code-Switching in LLM-based Speaking Practice
Junyeong Park, Jieun Han, Yeon Su Park, Youngbin Lee, Suin Kim, Juho Kim, Alice Oh, So-Yeon Ahn
Comments: Under review
Subjects: Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC)

Code-switching (CSW), the use of multiple languages within the same interaction, has been widely studied in NLP for multilingual communication. While CSW also occurs in language-learning contexts, the functions and pedagogical implications of learner CSW in learner-AI interactions remain underexplored. To address this gap, we introduce LAKE, a dataset of Learner-AI dialogues with Korean-English CSW. This dataset captures South Korean learners' CSW behavior during English speaking practice with LLM-based conversation partners, comprising 675 dialogues, 19.6K utterances, and 43.9 hours of learner speech. We develop a taxonomy of learner CSW functions, finding that learners switch to Korean for diverse purposes, including signaling lexical gaps, negotiating meaning, and conveying culturally specific content. We also observe learners reusing and adapting English expressions introduced by the LLM partner following their code-switches, suggesting opportunities for contextualized lexical support. To support research on speech recognition for learner CSW, we release 4.9 hours of code-switched learner speech with human-verified transcripts and benchmark speech-to-text models on Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), revealing difficulties in recognizing learner CSW. These findings highlight learner CSW as a communicative and pedagogically meaningful resource that can inform the design of AI-based conversational language learning systems.

[1024] arXiv:2601.09736 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Reinforced Linear Genetic Programming
