Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)

Robot manipulation often depends on short-term cues - such as brief contacts, temporary occlusions, and intermediate object states - that are ambiguous in a single frame and can only be resolved by integrating observations over time. However, injecting historical information solely by enlarging the history window is computationally costly and frequently yields limited gains due to substantial redundancy and task-agnostic, inflexible sampling of observations. We propose CondenseVLA, a multi-frame VLA policy with a learnable decoder-side history condensation module for using short-term visual context in action decoding. Given a sequence of cached per-frame features from the VLM backbone, CondenseVLA distills observation history into a fixed set of slot tokens using learnable queries and multi-head cross-attention. Simple auxiliary regularization penalizes overlap among slot attention maps and decorrelates slot embeddings, encouraging complementary attention and reducing slot redundancy. Across the evaluated tasks, CondenseVLA improves Simpler-WidowX success from 58.7% to 69.8% (+11.1 percentage points), achieves 97.2% on LIBERO, and reaches 52.8% on real-world tasks. It achieves 21.6% success on memory-dependent RMBench tasks. These results support selective condensation of bounded recent visual evidence for action decoding, while harder multi-observation tasks expose the limits of a finite history window. Project page: this https URL

[1363] arXiv:2610.25946 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Policy Search in Code Space for Multi-Agent Pathfinding
Matthias Eder, Pantelis Emmanouil, Vivek Farias, Fabian Fischer, Adam Jozefiak, Tianyi Peng, Thomas Ulz, Raphael Watschinger, Fangyu Wu, Andrew Zheng
Comments: 18 pages, 11 figures
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Developing coordination policies for complex multi-agent systems relies on either labor-intensive algorithm design or opaque task-specific reinforcement learning. With recent advances in autonomous coding agents, we show that policy search directly in code space offers a compelling third path that combines automated optimization with explicit interpretability. We investigate a human-directed workflow in which coding agents iteratively propose, implement, evaluate, diagnose, and eventually refine algorithms guided by simulation feedback and explicit correctness verification. We conducted two case studies and found that this workflow robustly outperformed any manually engineered solutions. On a challenging map in the 2024 League of Robot Runners competition, a two-day search discovered a policy that exceeds the stronger locally reproduced competition entry by 35.0% on the densest instance and generalizes to unseen map instances. In simulated real-world warehouses with irregular lanes, continuous robot geometry, and asynchronous motion, a week-long search discovered an entirely new class of multi-agent pathfinding algorithm that outperforms a calibrated proprietary solution in throughput by 58.9%. Under stated assumptions, we further prove that the new algorithm is collision-free and completes, in finite time, every accepted goal that is not withdrawn or replaced. Together, the studies show that policy search in code space powered by state-of-the-art coding agents offers a highly competitive path to building real engineering solutions that are both effective and analytically tractable.

[1364] arXiv:2610.25964 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Token-Set Choice Confounds POPE: A Systematic Audit of Yes/No Extraction in VLM Hallucination Evaluation
Kesav Kumar Jayakumar, Karthigeyan Thilak
Comments: NeurIPS 2026 VLM4RWD Workshop. 21 pages, 10 figures. Code: this https URL
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Computation and Language (cs.CL)

We set out to reproduce a recent hallucination-mitigation result on the POPE benchmark. The LLaVA-1.5-7B baseline we measured, 82.21 F1 on the adversarial split, sat 1.21 to 8.67 points above the adversarial baselines we planned to compare against (81.00, 79.30, and 73.54). We looked at the evaluation code and found a readout choice that moves F1 on its own. A two-token logit readout decides yes versus no by comparing two vocabulary IDs, 3582 ("yes") and 1217 ("no"). Across 9,000 greedy-decode questions spanning all three splits, neither ID is generated even once. The model emits " Yes" (token 3869) and " No" (token 1939), because SentencePiece prepends a space byte after the prompt suffix "ASSISTANT:". Read with an eight-token lookup that covers the space-prefixed surface forms, LLaVA-1.5-7B scores F1 0.8221, 0.8498, and 0.8713 on the adversarial, popular, and random splits. That 6.13-point adversarial shift exceeds the adversarial gain reported by five of the six papers we surveyed. None of them states its readout, and our reference ran under 4-bit NF4 quantization, so we cannot say how much of any reported gain a matched evaluation would keep. That comparison stays unresolved until readout and precision are matched. On the fixed baseline we run nine inference-time corrections of our own (none beat it) and dissect why the adversarial split resists logit-level intervention. In a 3,000-question probe, wrong predictions draw more image attention than correct ones (Cohen's $d=-0.46$, $p=1.4\times10^{-24}$), the opposite of what grounding-based corrections assume. A four-readout audit across four further VLMs from three tokenizer families confirms the confound is protocol-level, not model-specific: porting the LLaVA-1.5 IDs verbatim drops F1 to 0.00 on the two disjoint-vocabulary models, whereas a tokenizer-derived readout holds between 0.80 and 0.92.

[1365] arXiv:2610.26025 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: TamedFlow: Trajectory-Aware Distillation for Teacher-Assisted Diffusion Sampling
Shuaiqi Cheng, Jiahao Zhang, Boyuan Gu, Yuxi Chen, Haiying Xu, Zexin Lu, Huiyu Zhou, Xuming Hu
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) deliver high-fidelity image and video generation, but inference requires many sequential model evaluations. Two acceleration strategies are increasingly important: model compression makes each evaluation cheaper, while adaptive inference avoids selected teacher computation through reuse, forecasting, or speculative execution. Their combination, however, is brittle: directly applying the evaluated adaptive methods to a compressed student can degrade quality, an observed failure mode we call the \textbf{Combination Gap}. We link this gap to a mismatch between pointwise distillation and short-horizon execution: a student trained at teacher states need not remain reliable when its own predictions are chained. We propose \textbf{TamedFlow}, which trains a compressed DiT for this deployed role through cross-architecture feature alignment, a near-identity Velocity Alignment Head, and randomized rollout supervision. At inference, a lightweight Learnable Trajectory Estimator routes completed drafts: accepted drafts bypass the teacher, while rejected drafts roll back and receive one teacher rescue step. Distilling DiT-XL/2 into DiT-B/2, TamedFlow reaches FID $2.58$ at $2.25\times$ measured speedup over DDIM-50 on ImageNet $256\times256$. Ablations support trajectory supervision, and routing controls favor LTE over random decisions at nearly matched latency. Evaluations on ImageNet $512\times512$, MS-COCO, and Latte/FaceForensics extend the empirical scope.

[1366] arXiv:2610.26030 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Truncate or Not? A Scaling Study of Looped Transformers with Truncated Backpropagation
Xuyuan Xiong, Siyu Chen, Zihan Shao, Yue Su, Weiyang Jin, Ping Luo, Zhuoran Yang, Xihui Liu
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Machine Learning (stat.ML)

Looped transformers reuse a shared block of layers to increase computational depth without increasing the number of trainable parameters. They are trained with backpropagation through time (BPTT). To save training compute, BPTT is often truncated to the last few loops, but truncation yields biased gradients that may weaken the benefit of looping. In this work, we study the value of truncation in looped transformer training in a systematic way: we jointly vary model size, training tokens, and forward and backward loop counts across nearly 600 training runs and fit a unified scaling law that captures the effects of looping and truncation through effective parameters. Despite the training-compute savings of truncation, our fitted law favors full BPTT when forward and backward loop counts are jointly optimized. In matched-compute runs, full BPTT through fewer loops consistently outperforms truncated settings of the same compute. The law further shows that at fixed model size, the compute-optimal loop count and training-token budget both grow with compute. When model size is also free, the law identifies two fully trained loops as the best looped setting. Experimentally, this setting achieves lower validation loss than the compute-optimal non-looped model with about 27% fewer non-embedding parameters and only 8% more training compute.

[1367] arXiv:2610.26043 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: OmniInteract: Towards Unified Whole-Body Interaction Control for Dual Humanoids
Yinghao Li, Tianyu Zhang, Zhuohao Li, Yi-Lin Wei, Fa-Ting Hong, Qing Zhang, Wei-Shi Zheng
Comments: 30 pages including appendix, 11 figures. Project page: this https URL
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO)

Physical interaction is a key capability for humanoid collaboration, requiring coordinated whole-body motion and precise contact. However, learning diverse dual-humanoid interactions faces two major challenges: (1) human-robot morphological differences disrupt contact interfaces and spatial relationships during retargeting, and (2) jointly learning motor skills and partner coordination makes it difficult to retain control fidelity as interaction diversity grows. In this paper, we propose OmniInteract to address these challenges through surface-aware modeling and scalable residual policy learning. First, we introduce Surface Contact-Aware Retargeting, which leverages dense human-robot surface correspondences to jointly retarget both humanoids, preserving explicit interaction contact interfaces and their near-field geometric context. Second, we propose a Scalable Flow-based Interaction Policy for partner-conditioned residual generation. It factorizes dual-humanoid control into a reusable motor foundation and interaction-specific adaptations: partner-aware experts learn corrections over a frozen whole-body motion prior, while conditional flow matching unifies them in a shared residual action space. This enables scalable skill consolidation while retaining pretrained motor capabilities. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OmniInteract improves retargeting fidelity and dual-humanoid coordination while better retaining interaction performance as skill diversity grows. Real-world deployment further demonstrates successful contact establishment, stable whole-body coordination, and recovery from external perturbations.

[1368] arXiv:2610.26069 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Risk Decomposition for Hallucination-Aware Video Sampling
Chenyan Zheng, Fan Wu, Ruibo Li, Jiaxing Li, Minghao Yang, Bang Zhang, Guosheng Lin
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Despite achieving high visual fidelity, video models still suffer from physical hallucinations, limiting their reliability as world simulators. Existing methods leverage model-internal or external signals to improve physical plausibility, but their roles and limitations require a unified explanation. We propose a two-dimensional physical-hallucination risk framework that defines low-density sampling risk and high-density drifting risk. The first risk captures generations assigned low likelihood by the video model, for example, a ball suddenly teleporting despite the model favoring continuous motion, while the second risk captures physical inconsistencies in high-likelihood generations, for example, a ball bouncing progressively higher without additional energy. Our analysis explains how model-internal signals steer sampling toward higher-density regions of the learned distribution to address low-density sampling risk. However, higher model likelihood does not guarantee physical plausibility, motivating external guidance to address high-density drifting risk. Based on this framework, we develop Hallucination-Aware Sampler (HA-Sampler), which applies external physical guidance within latent refinement to generate physically plausible videos, and HA-Scorer, which derives a likelihood-based signal from the generator itself for evaluating generated videos using continuous normalizing flow (CNF), with coarse ODE integration and finite-difference divergence estimates. Experiments on Physics-IQ and VideoPhy benchmarks support our theoretical analysis and demonstrate that our methods outperform the compared sampling and scoring SOTA baselines.

[1369] arXiv:2610.26096 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: PnP-Transformer: A Neural Pose Solver for Zero-Shot 6D Object Pose Estimation
Emirkan Burak Yilmaz, Yakup Genc
Comments: Accepted to ECCV 2026 R6D Workshop
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

We present PnP-Transformer, a neural pose solver designed as an iterative-free, differentiable alternative to classical PnP-RANSAC algorithms. PnP-Transformer regresses the 6D object pose by processing predicted semi-dense 2D-3D correspondence fields alongside confidence scores, while mapping geometric inputs into a continuous latent space. To evaluate its practical utility, we integrate PnP-Transformer into a zero-shot 6D pose estimation pipeline, where the correspondence module and pose solver are trained separately. PnP-Transformer achieves a 41.2% mean AR score with low latency (0.46 s/obj) on seven core BOP benchmark datasets, surpassing all prior baselines (such as RayPose with 39.1% AR) but one (Co-op with 58.4% AR). When the pose solver is replaced with EPnP-RANSAC (similar to Co-op) while keeping the correspondence module unchanged, the RANSAC alternative outperforms PnP-Transformer on six of the seven datasets by reaching 52.2% mean AR at a cost of an additional 60 ms per object, revealing an accuracy-latency trade-off. Code and pretrained models are available at this https URL.

[1370] arXiv:2610.26179 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Learning Goal-Conditioned Subgoals through Frozen Hierarchical World Models
Xiang Kaibo, Liu Qingfeng
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Hierarchical world models plan over long horizons by passing predicted states from a coarse model to a lower-level controller. Choosing these states can be expensive: the upper-level planner repeatedly differentiates through candidate macro-action trajectories. We replace this search with a lightweight goal-conditioned network trained through the frozen high-level predictor. The network supplies a conditioning vector, while the predictor generates the next latent waypoint. Training uses hindsight goals and state-prediction losses on offline trajectories, without search-solution targets or macro-action labels. Inference retains an autoregressive high-level rollout, but requires no high-level candidate optimization. We evaluate this approach on the shared-latent HWM checkpoints distributed with H-JEPA, using three backbone seeds and three head initializations per backbone. With a common evaluation protocol, mean success is 70.4% on Cube, 48.7% on Push-T, 100.0% on FourRoom, and 71.1% on Visual AntMaze. The method improves over the corresponding HWM search baseline on three environments and has the same mean on Push-T. Dedicated measurements on an NVIDIA L40S give 1.28-4.39x end-to-end speedups for batched evaluation. Ablations identify state-adaptive conditioning as a consistent contributor, while predictor-mediated subgoals and unrestricted conditions have environment-dependent benefits.

[1371] arXiv:2610.26342 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: VibeTraining-Bench: Data-Trainer-Harness Co-Design for Iterative System Improvement
Ruotian Peng, Yuanyi Ren, Shuaiqi Liu, Xin Guo, Fang Zhu, Yangyi Huang, Yue Wu, Zheng Wang, Yandong Wen, Zhihang Fu
Comments: (Technical report (27 pages, 21 figures)
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Recursive self-improvement (RSI) requires agents to diagnose system bottlenecks and coordinate improvements across training and inference. We refer to the agents' capability to jointly optimize training data, the trainer, and the inference harness as cross-component co-design. We introduce VibeTraining-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating this capability across tasks spanning terminal operation, software engineering, multi-turn tool use, and mathematical reasoning. Within each task, research agents start from an identical initial agent system under a fixed resource budget. Guided by validation feedback, they iteratively refine data, trainers, and inference harnesses, then select and submit a final agent system for evaluation on the test set. To prevent reward hacking, we enforce three safeguards: test data isolation, separate research and grading containers, and network restrictions for research agents. Our evaluation results show that frontier research agents substantially improve target agent systems. For example, on SWE-bench Verified, GPT-6-Astra raises the target agent system's performance from 32.9% to 53.7%, comparable to the human-developed instruct model's 55.4%. However, there is still room to improve their ability to co-design and iteratively refine data, trainer, and harness to achieve cumulative performance gains. We hope that VibeTraining-Bench will serve as a unified platform for advancing RSI, deepening our understanding of cross-component optimization for agent systems. Code and data are available at this https URL.

[1372] arXiv:2610.26357 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: HGASurv: Hierarchical Granularity-Aware Multimodal Integration for Survival Prediction
Peike Yu, Wuchao Liu, Jihong Guan, Shuigeng Zhou
Comments: Preprint. Updated title, author notes, and manuscript presentation; reformatted using the Elsevier template
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Multimodal survival prediction jointly analyzes histopathological whole-slide images (WSIs), genomic profiles, and clinical variables to stratify patients by risk. However, existing approaches often inadequately account for granularity differences across modalities, particularly in spatial organization and feature dimensionality. Within pathology, aggregating WSI patch features without preserving their spatial arrangement can obscure tissue architecture; across modalities, directly concatenating low-dimensional clinical variables with high-dimensional visual and genomic features may limit the contribution of clinical information to prediction. To address these challenges, we propose HGASurv, which introduces a hierarchical WSI encoding module and a clinical-guided graph propagation module for granularity-aware multimodal integration. The hierarchical WSI encoding module maps WSI patch features onto a spatial grid using their original coordinates and applies parallel convolutions to construct representations at patch, local-neighborhood, and regional scales. Genomic signature embeddings then query these scale-specific WSI representations through cross-modal co-attention, producing signature-conditioned morphological features. The clinical-guided graph propagation module uses clinical variables to define patient-similarity edges and propagates fused image-genomic node embeddings with graph attention, integrating clinical information through topology rather than feature concatenation. Across three TCGA cohorts, HGASurv achieved the strongest overall C-index performance, with ablation studies supporting the complementary contributions of the hierarchical WSI encoding and clinical-guided graph propagation modules. This design shows that matching representation and integration mechanisms to modality-specific granularity improves multimodal survival prediction.

[1373] arXiv:2610.26407 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: A Simple and General Approach to top-$k$ Selection
Motti Goldberger, Nils Rudi
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Machine Learning (stat.ML)

This paper considers the Bayesian top-$k$ identification problem, wherein a decision maker is tasked with selecting $k$ items from a pool of items of unknown quality. To assess the items, the decision maker adaptively allocates a fixed sampling budget, where each sample of an item yields a noisy observation of its quality, with the objective of minimizing the expected opportunity cost of the selected set. We propose an approach that allocates each batch of samples by minimizing a surrogate objective derived from an upper bound on the expected opportunity cost. The approach is general: samples can be allocated in batches, the selection size $k$ is arbitrary, and it applies to many sampling distributions. It is also simple and intuitive. We prove that the method's posterior expected opportunity cost decays at an exponential rate of at least half the best rate achievable by any sampling rule. In simulations across a wide range of settings, the method is competitive with, and often improves upon, the best existing algorithm in each setting.

[1374] arXiv:2610.26443 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Rethinking LLM Fine-Tuning via Weight Space Reparameterization: Preserving Safety during Downstream Adaptation
Min-Seong Kim, Jongbok Won, Jeesup Park, Yonghee Choi, Dong-Jun Han
Comments: 32 pages, 5 figures. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026(spotlight)
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on downstream tasks often weakens their previously aligned safety behavior, creating an inherent trade-off between task adaptation and safety preservation. Existing approaches attempt to mitigate this issue by identifying safety-relevant neurons, layers, or update directions in the original parameter space. However, safety-related information is often distributed across many directions in this space, causing downstream updates to overwrite parameters that encode safety behavior. We propose WSR-Tune, a Weight Space Reparameterization-based fine-tuning framework that preserves safety during downstream adaptation. Our approach constructs a safety-conditioned basis and reparameterizes the weight matrices such that safety-relevant information becomes concentrated in a small subset of directions. We then identify safety-critical directions and freeze them in the reparameterized space, while updating the remaining complementary directions for downstream adaptation. By explicitly structuring the parameter space to disentangle safety and task information, our method reduces interference between objectives and enables simultaneous preservation of safety and improvement in downstream performance. Experimental results show that our method achieves a more favorable trade-off between downstream performance and safety retention, demonstrating its effectiveness for reliable LLM fine-tuning.

[1375] arXiv:2610.26636 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Revision-Based Learning from Interactive Experience and Feedback
Jiawen Li, Chenming Ge, Alice Gao, Rishab Vempati, Yi-Hao Peng, Jason Wu
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Code generation models are increasingly used to produce interactive artifacts, such as websites and user interfaces. Many properties that determine whether these interfaces are useful only become apparent through realistic interaction, making them difficult to incorporate into model training. In this paper, we introduce RELIEF (REvision-based Learning from Interactive Experience and Feedback), a method for improving code generation models using feedback on their generated interfaces. RELIEF uses a coding agent to revise these interfaces, then incorporates the improvements into their original generation traces to produce supervision for fine-tuning. To evaluate RELIEF, we collected a dataset of 200 synthetically generated websites paired with 355 interaction recordings and accompanying feedback from 24 users. We used critiques derived from code inspection, automated interaction, explicit human feedback, and human interaction recordings to fine-tune variants of two code generation models. Our results show that feedback effectiveness varies with base model capabilities, with critiques inferred from human interaction recordings leading to the largest usability improvements overall under our tested models.

[1376] arXiv:2610.26650 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: From Outcomes to Components: A Counterfactual Evaluation Framework for LLM-Proposed Repairs
Hengyu Ye, Songhua Hu
Comments: 27 pages, 5 figures, 15 tables. Code and data to be released with the camera-ready version
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL)

A repair action proposed by a large language model (LLM) specifies which records to change and how to change their values. A failed action may still contain a useful choice of records or a useful update, depending on how the two are paired. We introduce a counterfactual evaluation framework that separates selected records (targets) from the applied change (an update). Four executions combine proposed and reference targets and updates to measure the effects of correcting or retaining each component and their interaction. We evaluate the framework on two tasks: traffic assignment, where affected demand must be identified from road counts, and database repair, where affected rows must be identified from aggregate reports. An injected fault supplies a reference action that reverses it, and the recovery rate measures an action's loss reduction relative to that reference. For sparse-target actions in the traffic experiments, retaining the proposed update on reference targets achieves 79.4% of the reference loss reduction, compared with 43.7% from tuning update strength on the proposed targets. In the database experiments, update replacement worsens 17 of 108 actions, all selecting unaffected records, with sharply different frequencies across models. The value of a proposed update depends on the targets it is paired with. Missed targets hide useful updates, while excess targets can make a milder update better than the reference correction. In a component-reuse study, testing new target-update pairings from two proposals raises mean held-out recovery rate to 0.616, compared with 0.580 when selecting between the original proposals.

[1377] arXiv:2610.26659 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: SpatialScout: Can VLM Agents Actively Explore and Map 3D Scenes?

Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Spatial intelligence requires agents to actively acquire visual evidence and integrate observations into a coherent representation of the three-dimensional world. Yet spatial question answering offers limited evidence of whether models can construct accurate metric maps through autonomous exploration. We introduce SpatialScout, a benchmark for evaluating vision-language model (VLM) agents on active object-level 3D mapping. SpatialScout comprises 80 diverse indoor scenes containing 3,140 target objects. Given an object inventory, RGB observations, camera calibration, and camera poses, agents control a camera to explore each scene and estimate object centers in a shared coordinate frame. The task requires coordinating viewpoint selection, cross-view association, geometric estimation, and map revision under bounded interaction budgets. Evaluation jointly measures localization accuracy and target coverage through object-scale overlap scores that penalize missing predictions. Experiments with frontier VLMs reveal substantial limitations: the strongest evaluated model, Claude Opus 5.5, achieves a mean overlap score of 41.71%, with 47.23% of targets exceeding an intersection-over-union (IoU) threshold of 0.5 and only 3.25% exceeding 0.9. These results reveal a substantial gap between recovering coarse object layouts and constructing complete, precise metric maps. SpatialScout provides a quantitative testbed for developing agents that build reliable 3D spatial representations through active perception. Code is available at this https URL.

[1378] arXiv:2610.26680 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Robotic Physical Comparison of Biologically Motivated and Counterfactual Sensory Arrangements using Biomimetic Skin
Akihiro Miki, Shun Hasegawa, Yoshimoto Ribayashi, Yuta Sahara, Kento Kawaharazuka, Kei Okada
Comments: Published in Bioinspiration & Biomimetics (IOP Publishing). Project page: this https URL Youtube: this https URL

Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO)

Human skin contains diverse mechanoreceptors, including Merkel cells and Pacinian corpuscles, each localized in specific regions. Although their spatial organization is known to be shaped by molecular signaling and neural induction during development, experimentally examining its functional significance under controlled conditions in living systems remains challenging. In particular, physically comparing alternative receptor arrangements that do not occur biologically is difficult. In this study, we developed a layered biomimetic robotic skin designed to mimic key structural features of human skin tissue by embedding receptor-analog sensors within compliant soft media. Using this platform, we implemented both biologically motivated and counterfactual sensory arrangements and quantitatively evaluated their performance across three passive tactile tasks: detection of weak contacts, a two-point discrimination-like assessment, and texture identification. Arrangements reflecting key features of the biologically motivated sensory organization exhibited higher performance than the alternative configurations examined. This study addresses a biological question concerning how spatial organization influences tactile function by presenting a biomimetic robotic approach that enables physical and empirical comparison of biologically motivated and counterfactual sensory arrangements that are difficult to investigate in living systems.

[1379] arXiv:2610.26770 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs

Comments: 41 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables, under review
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Harness development plays a crucial role in building capable AI agents. Recent approaches improve harnesses through recursive self-improvement (RSI), but their performance gains often come with higher execution costs. We introduce HarnessPro, a label-free method for evolving harnesses to improve task performance while reducing execution cost. In this setting, candidate harnesses are evaluated using LLM-generated tests without access to ground-truth solutions or official tests. Specialized agents diagnose execution trajectories, plan updates with different performance-cost priorities, and implement them as candidate harnesses. Rather than returning a single harness, HarnessPro uses normalized weighted squared-distance selection to provide cost-focused (lite), balanced (medium), and performance-focused (heavy) harnesses for different deployment budgets. Selected harnesses enter the next iteration, where execution feedback guides further updates. Our experiments cover Terminal-Bench 2, SWE-Bench Pro, and ProgramBench, using GPT-5.5 with Codex and GLM-5.2 with Claude Code. Across these benchmarks using GPT-5.5 with Codex, the heavy mode of HarnessPro achieves an average pass-rate gain of 2.0 percentage points and an average per-task cost reduction of 26.1% relative to RHO. This advantage also holds when using GLM-5.2 with Claude Code. Code is available at this https URL

[1380] arXiv:2610.26820 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Open-Form Geometric Style Transfer
Adar Elad, Gal Metzer, Omer Dahary, Min Lu, Daniel Cohen-Or
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Graphics (cs.GR)

A geometric style learned from one family of shapes is typically applied to new shapes from the same family. We consider a more challenging setting: learning the geometric design language of a stylized Latin alphabet and applying it to new forms, from Greek glyphs to entirely different structures such as human poses. We introduce Open-Form Geometric Style Transfer, where the forms to which a learned geometric style can be applied are not restricted to the shape family in which that style was observed. This setting is deceptively challenging: the difficulty is not merely learning a style, but learning the style without learning the shape family in which it was observed. We represent target forms by structural sketches and disentangle structural adherence from style realization using a Geometry LoRA and a style-specific LoRA. Critically, open-form transfer requires the Geometry LoRA to be universal. To achieve this, we devise a geometry-enrichment strategy that constructs a large and purposefully diverse collection of synthetic structural sketches spanning a broad range of unfamiliar geometries. Our experiments and ablations demonstrate the importance of both disentanglement and this universal geometry prior, enabling geometric styles learned from glyphs, pictograms, and other shape families to be transferred to substantially different, unseen forms.

Memory-native evolution requires making memory an intrinsic capability of foundation models, enabling them to continuously accumulate and utilize information. To this end, we introduce MemT-1.0, a new architecture of memory foundation models that internalize memory as part of model computation. Building on Metis, MemT-1.0 employs Gated DeltaNet-2 with a stable token-level memory update mechanism within each turn. We further introduce Mixture-of-Storage to scale native memory capacity. Following a deliberate backbone preparation, we develop a two-stage training pipeline consisting of continued pre-training and post-training, supported by 34B tokens of training data and efficient training and inference infrastructure. We release a model family comprising MemT-1.0-Nano and MemT-1.0-Flash, and conduct a comprehensive evaluation of memory and general capabilities. The results show that they outperform the parametric memory baselines on average and remain competitive with retrieval-augmented methods, while largely preserving general capabilities. At a history length of 128K tokens, MemT-1.0-Nano achieves approximately $1.86\times$ end-to-end inference speedup and a $66\times$ reduction in persistent storage relative to full context KV cache. By internalizing retrieved procedural experience, MemT-1.0 improves task success on agentic tasks, providing a practical step toward memory-native evolution.

[1382] arXiv:2610.26847 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: WeAct: Dynamic Weight Switching as Agent Actions
Rui Shi, Xunjian Yin, Jiacheng Sang, Zichuan Liu, Shuyan Zhou
Comments: 24 pages, 14 figures, 12 tables, including references and appendices
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Long-horizon agents must learn heterogeneous capabilities from interleaved trajectories. Updating shared parameters to learn new capabilities can degrade previously acquired ones, resulting in catastrophic forgetting. As a trajectory unfolds, different stages may require different capabilities, yet conventional joint training and static adapter merging maintain a fixed parameter configuration throughout execution. We introduce WeAct (Weight-level Internal Actions), which trains independent capability-specific LoRA adapters over a frozen backbone and adds adapter selection to the agent's action space. These internal actions use the model's native tool-calling interface for on-demand capability composition in a shared context. Across eight deep-research benchmarks, Qwen3-32B with WeAct improves average accuracy by 6.2% relative to full fine-tuning counterparts despite using less compute, and by 27.5% relative to the strongest static LoRA-merging method. WeAct also supports modular continual adaptation, by adding a new code computation adapter to expand the agent's capabilities and updating the existing writing adapter to improve report quality. Both updates leave the backbone and other adapters unchanged, supporting modular continual adaptation in agents.

[1383] arXiv:2610.26853 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: InfiniDream: Open-Ended Photorealistic 3D Worlds Through Procedural Generation

Comments: Project page: this https URL
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Procedural generation plays a key role in synthetic data creation and game development, offering greater controllability, editability, and diversity than static mesh representations. However, VLM-based code generation often produces relatively simple 3D assets, while sophisticated photorealistic procedural systems require extensive manual development. Existing VLM-guided procedural methods remain largely constrained by predefined factories and APIs, limiting their ability to create novel asset types. We introduce InfiniDream, a VLM-driven framework for open-ended procedural 3D world generation. First, we propose Symbolically Constrained Asset Generation, which leverages existing procedural algorithms to create novel, photorealistic assets while preserving editability and seed-based diversity. Second, we develop an end-to-end text-to-world pipeline that combines semantic scene planning with Deterministic Frustum-Guided Grid Placement to construct large-scale 3D worlds with precise object placement, procedural population, and animation. Extensive evaluations on 100 object and 20 scene generation tasks demonstrate improvements across four perceptual metrics. Diversity analysis, ablation studies, and human preference evaluations further validate the effectiveness of our framework. Project page: this https URL

[1384] arXiv:2610.26854 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Physical Words: A Vocabulary for Structuring Latent Reasoning in Robot Manipulation

Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO)

Multimodal reasoning provides robotic foundation models with predictive context needed for reliable action generation. However, language-based reasoning captures task semantics but struggles to express fine-grained physical dynamics, while latent reasoning models future state evolution but offers limited structure for organizing these dynamics into reusable reasoning primitives. To bridge this gap, we introduce PhysWord, a reasoning-before-acting foundation model built on Physical Words, which use atomic action verbs as shared semantic anchors for continuous representations of physical dynamics. Specifically, PhysWord predicts upcoming atomic action words and directly aligns their contextual hidden states with latent targets derived from the corresponding future observations. Building on these primitives, we construct a temporally structured PhysWord space with visual and optional tactile variants of each action word. Autoregressively predicting Physical Words across future timesteps captures transitions between execution stages, providing structured multimodal context for action generation. PhysWord achieves state-of-the-art success rates of 90.3\% on visuotactile UniVTAC and 99.6\% on vision-based LIBERO-Long, and outperforms competing methods on real-world tasks using bimanual grippers and dexterous hands. Further evaluations demonstrate that our structured latent reasoning framework generalizes to unseen scenarios and enables long-horizon manipulation.

[1385] arXiv:2610.26863 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Text-to-Image Generative Modeling Without Language Pretraining

Halcyon also learns image captioning by replacing caption dropout with I2T supervision, maintaining competitive T2I generation quality under the same pretraining budget. [1386] arXiv:1809.05643 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]

Subjects: Computational Finance (q-fin.CP); Numerical Analysis (math.NA); Probability (math.PR)

We study kernel-based collocation methods for numerical solutions of Heath-Jarrow-Morton models in Musiela parametrization. The methods are Euler-Maruyama approximations of finite-dimensional stochastic differential equations and can be used with standard Monte Carlo procedures for derivative pricing. [1387] arXiv:2310.14421 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Entropic perspective on AI resilience, data-minimal learning and optimal control
Illia Horenko
Subjects: Machine Learning (stat.ML); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Behind the general terms like adversarial attacks and generative adversarial networks (GANs), such criteria as AI resilience and AI robustness gained a crucial importance, in trying to make the emergent AI tools reliable, energy-efficient and safe. From mathematical perspective, these problems boil down to finding a mathematically-sound quantification of the smallest-sufficient amounts of the perturbations of function arguments that lead to the largest possible perturbations of the approximated function values. Here, the entropy-optimising perspective on adversarial algorithms from Artificial Intelligence (AI) is proposed to attack this problem. It is shown that adopting this perspective helps proving computational conditions for the global optimality and uniqueness of adversarial attacks based on cheaply-verifiable mathematical criteria. Further, it is shown how this perspective can be used for developing self-attacking learning algorithms, that generate optimal new data points for training, replacing one of the trained agents with this mathematical criterium. On a broad selection of various synthetic and real-life problems from hydrodynamics and biomedicine, it is shown that such self-attacking learning algorithms allow training orders-of-magnitude simpler and cheaper models with superior performance - and can be used to directly train the optimal controls in complex systems, requiring only a small fraction of the training data and outperforming the as-comprehensive-as-the-author-was-able-to-find set of contemporary AI tools (like boosted Random Forests, deep neural networks, foundational models based on transformer architectures, etc.) in complexity (measured as the model descriptor length) and predictive performance.}

[1388] arXiv:2406.04203 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Explicit Steady-State Approximations for Parallel Server Systems with Heterogeneous Servers
Yaosheng Xu
Subjects: Probability (math.PR); Systems and Control (eess.SY); Optimization and Control (math.OC)

We study the steady-state performance of parallel-server systems under an immediate routing architecture with two sources of heterogeneity: server types and job classes, often subject to compatibility constraints. We focus on the weighted-workload-task-allocation (WWTA) routing policy, a load-balancing scheme known to be throughput-optimal for such systems. Under a relaxed complete-resource-pooling (CRP) condition, we prove a strong form of state-space collapse in heavy traffic and that the scaled server workloads jointly converge in distribution to a deterministic vector multiplied by an exponential random variable, whose mean is explicitly given by system primitives. Our analysis yields three main insights. First, the conventional heavy-traffic assumption of a unique static allocation plan can be dropped; a relaxed CRP condition suffices. Second, the limiting workload distribution is shown to be independent of the local scheduling policies at the servers, allowing substantial flexibility. Third, the inefficient (non-basic) activities identified by the static allocation problem are proved to receive an asymptotically negligible fraction of routed jobs and service effort, even though WWTA has no prior knowledge of which activities are non-basic, highlighting its robustness to changing arrival rates.

[1389] arXiv:2408.16189 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Help Me Help You: The Aggregate Value of Source and Target Data in Transfer Learning
Steve Hanneke, Samory Kpotufe
Comments: This is a revision of a work previously posted to arXiv in 2024 by the same authors under the same arXiv number with a different title. The current version is revised to better highlight the key contributions. No AI was used in the production of this work
Subjects: Machine Learning (stat.ML); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Statistics Theory (math.ST)

Transfer learning, in regression or classification, concerns problems where one aims to use imperfect data from a source distribution P to improve prediction w.r.t. a target distribution Q. While there is now much theoretical understanding of the unsupervised setting of this problem (where no labeled target data is available), the supervised setting with labeled target data remains under-studied.
We identify and characterize an interesting dichotomy in the rates achievable in the supervised setting: there is a weak transfer regime where optimal rates are determined by information in either the source or target dataset but not both, and a strong transfer regime where much faster target rates are achievable, accounting for complementary information in source and target data. Furthermore, while previous theoretical tools for the unsupervised setting can be extended to capture the weak transfer regime, we argue that they cannot capture the strong regime due to limitations inherent in the various notions of relatedness they rely on. Instead, we provide an appropriate refinement of relatedness notions---termed weak and strong moduli of transfer---that reveal the two regimes and lead to a nontrivial characterization of which pairs of distributions P and Q adhere to which regime.
Finally, the above dichotomy reveals a new categorization of existing algorithmic approaches in terms of their optimality or lack-thereof across supervised regimes, and we provide a generic approach that remains nearly optimal in all regimes without prior distributional knowledge.

[1390] arXiv:2412.02591 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Persistent (Co)Homology in Matrix Multiplication Time
Dmitriy Morozov, Primoz Skraba
Comments: Fast row algorithms corrected
Subjects: Algebraic Topology (math.AT); Computational Complexity (cs.CC)

Most algorithms for computing persistent homology do so by tracking cycles that represent homology classes. There are many choices of such cycles, and specific choices have found different uses in applications. Although it is known that persistence diagrams can be computed in matrix multiplication time [8] for the more general case of zigzag persistent homology, it is not clear how to extract cycle representatives, especially if specific representatives are desired. In this paper, we provide the same matrix multiplication bound for computing representatives for the two choices common in applications in the case of ordinary persistent (co)homology. We first provide a fast version of the reduction algorithm, which is simpler than the algorithm in [8], but returns a different set of representatives than the standard algorithm [6] We then give a fast version of a different variant called the row algorithm [4], which returns the same representatives as the standard algorithm.

[1391] arXiv:2412.05691 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Undergraduate Course Allocation through Competitive Markets
Daniel Kornbluth, Alexey Kushnir
Subjects: Theoretical Economics (econ.TH); Computer Science and Game Theory (cs.GT)

Prevailing methods of course allocation at undergraduate institutions involve reserving seats to give priority to designated groups of students. We present a competitive equilibrium-based mechanism that assigns course seats using student preferences and course priorities. This mechanism satisfies approximate notions of stability, efficiency, envy-freeness, and strategy-proofness. We evaluate its performance relative to a mechanism widely used in practice using preferences estimated from university data. Our empirical findings demonstrate an improvement in student satisfaction and allocation fairness. The number of students who envy another student of weakly lower priority declines by 8 percentage points, or roughly 500 students.

[1392] arXiv:2502.07585 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: On the existence of pure epsilon-equilibria
Bary S.R. Pradelski, Bassel Tarbush
Subjects: Theoretical Economics (econ.TH); Computer Science and Game Theory (cs.GT)

Departing from optimizing behavior by any $\epsilon>0$ ensures the existence of stable outcomes in a broad class of many-agent games where utilities are drawn from a joint distribution. Specifically, in a game with iid drawn utilities from a continuous distribution and any $\epsilon>0$, we show that as the number of agents gets large the probability that a pure $\epsilon$-equilibrium exists converges to 1, while, by contrast, the probability that a pure Nash equilibrium exists is known to converge to $1-1/e\approx 0.63$. The asymptotic existence of pure $\epsilon$-equilibrium extends to utilities that are negatively correlated across agents, and we identify a correlation threshold dependent on $\epsilon$ that is tight for the zero-sum case. We also study the cases of correlation across action profiles and of utility ties and, in all cases, we also characterize the asymptotic distribution of pure $\epsilon$-equilibria. Regarding pure Nash equilibrium---i.e., when $\epsilon=0$---our results nest, organize, and extend the existing literature. All our results and those from the prior literature are applications of our ``master theorem'', which builds on the Chen--Stein method and Stein's method.

[1393] arXiv:2502.16260 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Assortment optimization given basket shopping behavior using the Ising model
Andrey Vasilyev, Sebastian Maier, Ralf W. Seifert
Subjects: Optimization and Control (math.OC); Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS)

In markets where customers tend to purchase baskets of products rather than single products, assortment optimization is a major challenge for retailers. Removing a product from a retailer's assortment can result in a severe drop in aggregate demand if this product is a complement to other products. Therefore, accounting for the complementarity effect is essential when making assortment decisions. In this paper, we develop an analytical framework designed to address this problem. We model customers' choices using the binary Ising model, which is a special case of a Markov random field. This model captures pairwise demand dependencies as well as the individual attractiveness of each product, with binary variables indicating whether products are included in the purchased basket. For estimation, we utilize existing methods developed for the spin formulation of the Ising model and then apply a parameter transformation to express the fitted model in the binary form used for assortment optimization. We show that the assortment optimization problem under the Ising model is NP-hard. We also provide multiple theoretical insights into the structure of the optimal assortments based on the graphical representation of the Ising model, and propose several heuristic algorithms that can be used to obtain high-quality solutions to the assortment optimization problem. Our numerical analysis demonstrates that the developed simulated annealing procedure leads to an expected profit gain of 15% compared to offering an unoptimized assortment (where all products are included) and around 5% compared to using a revenue-ordered heuristic algorithm.

[1394] arXiv:2509.14203 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Bellman Optimality of Average-Reward Robust Markov Decision Processes with a Constant Gain
Shengbo Wang, Nian Si
Subjects: Optimization and Control (math.OC); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Learning and optimal control under robust Markov decision processes (MDPs) have received increasing attention, yet most existing theory, algorithms, and applications focus on finite-horizon or discounted models. Long-run average-reward formulations, while natural in many operations research and management contexts, remain underexplored. This is primarily because the dynamic programming foundations are technically challenging and only partially understood, with several fundamental questions remaining open. This paper steps toward a general framework for average-reward robust MDPs by analyzing the constant-gain setting. We study the average-reward robust control problem with possible information asymmetries between the controller and an S-rectangular adversary. Our analysis centers on the constant-gain robust Bellman equation, examining both the existence of solutions and their relationship to the optimal average reward. Specifically, we identify when solutions to the robust Bellman equation characterize the optimal average reward and stationary policies, and we provide one-sided weak communication conditions ensuring solutions' existence. These findings expand the dynamic programming theory for average-reward robust MDPs and lay a foundation for robust dynamic decision making under long-run average criteria in operational environments.

[1395] arXiv:2509.21469 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: On the hardness of approximating minimum distances of quantum codes
Elena Grigorescu, Vatsal Jha, Eric Samperton
Comments: Accepted to FSTTCS25
Subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph); Computational Complexity (cs.CC); Information Theory (cs.IT)

The problem of computing distances of error-correcting codes is fundamental in both the classical and quantum settings. While hardness for the classical version of these problems has been known for some time (in both the exact and approximate settings), it was only recently that Kapshikar and Kundu showed the hardness of these problems for non-degenerate quantum codes. As our first main result, we get a direct reduction to CSS codes, the most commonly used type of quantum code, from the minimum distance problem for classical linear codes. In particular, our proof uses arguably simpler constructions based on hypergraph product codes.
Our second set of results considers the distance of a graph state, which is a key parameter for quantum codes obtained via the codeword stabilized formalism. We show that it is NP-hard to compute/approximate the distance of a graph state, which is a degenerate quantum code, when the adjacency matrix of the graph is the input. This establishes hardness for even degenerate quantum codes, which was not known before. Furthermore, we show this is true even if we only consider X-type errors of a graph state. Our techniques, moreover, imply an interesting classical consequence: the hardness of computing or approximating the distance of classical codes with rate equal to 1/2.
One of the main motivations of the present work is a question raised by Kapshikar and Kundu concerning the NP-hardness of approximation when there is an additive error proportional to a quantum code's length. We show that no such hardness can hold for hypergraph product codes. These observations suggest the possibility of a new kind of square root barrier.

[1396] arXiv:2510.06919 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Bayesian Nonparametric Dynamical Clustering of Time Series

Comments: Revised version with methodological refinements, expanded experimental results, and improvements to the presentation
Subjects: Machine Learning (stat.ML); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Applications (stat.AP)

We present a method that models the evolution of an unbounded number of time series clusters by switching among an unknown number of regimes with linear dynamics. We develop a Bayesian non-parametric approach using a hierarchical Dirichlet process as a prior on the parameters of a Switching Linear Dynamical System and a Gaussian process prior to model the statistical variations in amplitude and temporal alignment within each cluster. By modeling the evolution of time series patterns, the method avoids unnecessary proliferation of clusters in a principled manner. We perform inference by formulating a variational lower bound for off-line and on-line scenarios, enabling efficient learning through optimization. We illustrate the versatility and effectiveness of the approach through several case studies of electrocardiogram analysis using publicly available databases.

[1397] arXiv:2510.08361 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Isolation of non-triangle cycles in graphs
Peter Borg, Dayle Scicluna
Comments: 12 pages, 1 figure, minor corrections made
Journal-ref: Discrete Applied Mathematics 394 (2026), 261-268
Subjects: Combinatorics (math.CO); Discrete Mathematics (cs.DM)

Given a set $\mathcal{F}$ of graphs, we call a copy of a graph in $\mathcal{F}$ an $\mathcal{F}$-graph. The $\mathcal{F}$-isolation number of a graph $G$, denoted by $\iota(G, \mathcal{F})$, is the size of a smallest set $D$ of vertices of $G$ such that the closed neighbourhood $N[D]$ of $D$ intersects the vertex sets of the $\mathcal{F}$-graphs contained by $G$ (equivalently, $G-N[D]$ contains no $\mathcal{F}$-graph). Let $\mathcal{C}$ be the set of cycles, and let $\mathcal{C}'$ be the set of non-triangle cycles (that is, cycles of length at least $4$). Let $G$ be a connected graph having exactly $n$ vertices and $m$ edges. The first author proved that $\iota(G,\mathcal{C}) \leq n/4$ if $G$ is not a triangle. Bartolo and the authors determined a set $\mathcal{E}_4$ of nine graphs such that $\iota(G,\{C_4\}) \leq n/5$ if $G$ is not an $\mathcal{E}_4$-graph. Chen and Cui recently strengthened this result by proving that $\iota(G, \mathcal{C}') \leq n/5$ if $G$ is not an $\mathcal{E}_4$-graph. This had been proved by Zhang and Wu for the case where $G$ contains no triangle. Various authors proved that $\iota(G,\mathcal{C}) \leq (m+1)/5$ if $G$ is not a triangle. We prove that $\iota(G,\mathcal{C}') \leq (m+1)/6$ if $G$ is not a $4$-cycle. Zhang and Wu established this for the case where $G$ contains no triangle. Our result yields the inequality $\iota(G,\{C_4\}) \leq (m+1)/6$ of Wei, Zhang and Zhao. These bounds are attained by infinitely many (non-isomorphic) graphs. The proof of our inequality hinges on also determining the graphs attaining the bound.

[1398] arXiv:2512.10570 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: FLEXI-Haz: Semiparametric Deep Survival Inference Beyond Proportional Hazards
Asaf Ben Arie, Malka Gorfine
Subjects: Machine Learning (stat.ML); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Flexible survival prediction does not by itself ensure valid inference for covariate effects or subject-specific survival probabilities. We develop FLEXI-Haz, a semiparametric deep neural network model for right-censored data that combines an interpretable linear component in the log-hazard with a flexible function of time and adjustment covariates. This formulation permits nonproportional nuisance effects while retaining interpretable regression parameters. Under regularity conditions, we establish nuisance convergence rates that are minimax optimal up to logarithmic factors over composite Holder classes, together with root-n-consistent, asymptotically normal, and semiparametrically efficient estimation of the regression parameter. For adjustment covariates with finite support, we derive the explicit influence function for cumulative hazard and construct a cross-fitted one-step estimator yielding asymptotically valid pointwise confidence intervals for subject-specific survival. Simulations demonstrate reduced bias and improved coverage relative to a proportional hazards comparator under time-varying nuisance effects. An analysis of the Rotterdam breast cancer data illustrates the consequences of flexible adjustment for inference on treatment associations.

[1399] arXiv:2512.19003 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Four Function Theorems Through Optimal Transport and Entropic Analogs
Mokshay Madiman, James Melbourne, Cyril Roberto
Subjects: Probability (math.PR); Information Theory (cs.IT); Functional Analysis (math.FA)

We study entropic versions of four-function inequalities and give transport proofs of the Euclidean Ahlswede-Daykin theorem and a four-function version of the Prekopa-Leindler inequality due to Cordero-Erausquin and Maurey. One of our main results shows that the sharp range for the four-function inequality for equally weighted power means of finite orders \(\alpha,\beta\) is \(0\leq\alpha+\beta\leq2\), with the Ahlswede-Daykin min-max inequality obtained as a limit. En route, we prove corresponding entropy inequalities under the quadratic optimal transport coupling, including an entropy power inequality for the minimum and maximum in Euclidean space. We also study the stability of four-function inequalities under convolution with log-concave product densities, recovering the preservation of log-supermodularity established by Karlin and Rinott, and explain its application to a conditional entropy power inequality for log-supermodular random variables.

[1400] arXiv:2512.23917 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Tensor computing application programming interface: An application-oriented, lightweight API for portable high-performance tensor network computations
Rong-Yang Sun, Tomonori Shirakawa, Hidehiko Kohshiro, D. N. Sheng, Seiji Yunoki
Comments: 46 pages, 10 figures
Subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph); Strongly Correlated Electrons (cond-mat.str-el); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Tensor networks (TNs) are a central computational tool in quantum science and artificial intelligence. However, the lack of a unified software interface across tensor-computing frameworks severely limits the portability of TN applications, coupling algorithmic development to specific hardware and software back ends. To address this challenge, we introduce the Tensor Computing Application Programming Interface (TCAPI)---an application-oriented, lightweight API designed to enable framework-independent, high-performance TN applications, currently specified for \texttt{C++} and \texttt{Python}. TCAPI provides well-defined type-system conventions that abstract tensor objects, together with a minimal yet expressive set of core functions for essential tensor manipulations and tensor linear-algebra operations, with operation semantics shared across language specifications. Through numerical demonstrations of representative tensor-network applications implemented in \texttt{C++} using TCAPI, we show that code written against TCAPI can be migrated seamlessly across heterogeneous hardware and software platforms while achieving performance comparable to native framework implementations. We further provide open-source implementations of TCAPI based on \textit{Cytnx} and \textit{ITensor} in \texttt{C++}, and on \textit{NumPy} in \texttt{Python}, demonstrating its practicality and ease of integration with existing tensor-computing frameworks.

[1401] arXiv:2602.04943 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Graph-Theoretic Analysis of Phase Optimization Complexity in Variational Wave Functions for Heisenberg Antiferromagnets
Mahmud Ashraf Shamim, Md Moshiur Rahman Raj, Mohamed Hibat-Allah, Paulo T Araujo
Comments: The NP-hardness claim has been corrected, and the connection to variational Monte Carlo has been revised
Subjects: Strongly Correlated Electrons (cond-mat.str-el); Disordered Systems and Neural Networks (cond-mat.dis-nn); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computational Complexity (cs.CC); Quantum Physics (quant-ph)

We study the computational complexity of learning the ground state phase structure of Heisenberg antiferromagnets. Representing Hilbert space as a weighted graph, the variational energy defines a weighted XY model that, for $\mathbb{Z}_2$ phases, reduces to a classical antiferromagnetic Ising model on that graph. For fixed amplitudes, reconstructing the signs of the ground state wavefunction thus reduces to a weighted Max-Cut instance. This links sign optimization of wavefunctions directly to combinatorial optimization.

[1402] arXiv:2603.03188 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Scalable Posterior Uncertainty for Flexible Density-Based Clustering
Nicola Bariletto, Stephen G. Walker
Subjects: Machine Learning (stat.ML); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Density-based clustering is a well-established framework that defines clusters through topological or geometric features of the data-generating density, yielding flexible procedures that have proven effective on large and complex datasets. We address the problem of obtaining scalable Bayesian-style uncertainty quantification by combining density-based clustering with martingale posterior distributions. Density uncertainty is first quantified through a fully parallelized predictive resampling scheme driven by model score functions, naturally accommodating modern differentiable density estimators such as normalizing flows. Posterior samples of the clustering are then obtained by applying density-based clustering to each random density sampled from the martingale posterior, enabling inference on any clustering-related quantity. Casting the estimand as a density functional also enables a rigorous frequentist convergence analysis. We illustrate the method through applications to image and single-cell RNA sequencing data, where it recovers meaningful clustering structures, including the assignment of previously unseen data and biologically interpretable cell grouping, while running in minutes on a single GPU.

[1403] arXiv:2603.26029 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Detection Is Harder Than Estimation in Certain Regimes: Inference for Moment and Cumulant Tensors
Runshi Tang, Yuefeng Han, Anru R. Zhang
Subjects: Statistics Theory (math.ST); Computational Complexity (cs.CC)

We study estimation and detection of high-order cumulant tensors from $n$ i.i.d. observations of a $p$-dimensional random vector, with performance measured in the tensor spectral norm. Under sub-Gaussianity, we show that the minimax rate for estimating the order-$d$ cumulant tensor is $\sqrt{p/n}\wedge 1$. In contrast to covariance estimation, the natural plug-in estimator obtained by replacing population moments in the moment--cumulant formula with sample moments, which we call the sample cumulant tensor, is generally not rate-optimal for $d\ge 3$, and we construct an estimator that attains the minimax rate. On the computational side, we study testing whether the $d$-th order cumulant tensor vanishes after whitening. We provide evidence, under a model-specific low-degree conjecture, that detection is computationally hard when $n\ll p^{d/2}$. At the same time, we identify a regime in which an efficiently computable estimator achieves error smaller than the separation at which polynomial-time tests can reliably distinguish the null from the alternative under the same conjecture. This reveals an unusual reverse detection--estimation gap: computationally efficient detection can be harder than computationally efficient estimation. The underlying reason is that the relevant loss, tensor spectral norm, is itself NP-hard to compute, creating a new form of computational--statistical gap.

[1404] arXiv:2605.18587 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: PACE: Geometry-Aware Bridge Transport for Single-Cell Trajectory Inference
Chenglei Yu, Chuanrui Wang, Bangyan Liao, Tailin Wu
Comments: NeurIPS 2026. 32 pages, 12 figures
Subjects: Genomics (q-bio.GN); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Single-cell trajectory inference from destructive time-course snapshots is fundamentally ill-posed: neither cross-time cell correspondences nor continuous trajectories are observed, so the snapshot distributions alone do not uniquely determine the underlying dynamics. Existing optimal transport and flow-based methods typically couple cells by Euclidean proximity at observed clock times, which can misalign trajectories when development is asynchronous and cells sampled at the same experimental time occupy different latent pseudotime stages. We propose PACE, a trajectory inference framework that recovers geometry-consistent continuous transport dynamics from destructive time-course snapshots through three coupled components. First, PACE constructs a state- and time-dependent anisotropic Riemannian metric that assigns low transport cost along locally supported tangent directions while penalizing normal velocity components. Second, it alternates between refining cross-time couplings under the induced path-action cost and fitting endpoint-preserving neural bridges between adjacent snapshots. Third, it distills the learned bridge dynamics into a global continuous-time velocity field over cellular states. Across seven controlled and biological datasets covering nine held-out reconstruction experiments, PACE achieves the strongest overall reconstruction performance, reducing MMD, Wasserstein-1 distance, and Wasserstein-2 distance by 23.7% on average relative to the strongest competing baseline. PACE also improves RNA-velocity alignment by 15.4% on an embryoid body differentiation benchmark, without requiring explicit cell pairing, lineage tracing, or RNA-velocity supervision during training. Code is available at this https URL.

[1405] arXiv:2605.25066 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: QML-PipeGuard: Detecting Channel-Substitution Attacks on Quantum Machine Learning Pipelines in Untrusted Clouds
Esra Yeniaras
Comments: 30 pages, 4 figures. Extended version of a paper accepted at NordSec 2026 (Springer LNCS). Contains the full appendices omitted from the proceedings version for length. Supersedes v1: the detection and drift guarantees are now stated at the marginal level with a tight constant, and the finite-shot analysis controls both error directions
Subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph); Cryptography and Security (cs.CR); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

As machine-learning workloads move onto quantum hardware they inherit a trust problem classical AI deployments have largely solved and quantum ones have not: quantum machine learning (QML) is already sold as a cloud service, and a customer cannot check that the circuit they paid for is actually the circuit that ran. We show the gap is exploitable. A malicious or cost-cutting provider can substitute the declared quantum channel with one that reproduces every accuracy test the customer performs, passes the single-observable checks used in practice, and still differs from the declared computation at the channel level. We call this a channel-substitution attack and instantiate it in three deployments: audit evasion, service downgrade, and result forgery in reproducibility review. QML-PipeGuard detects the attack at runtime from measurement statistics the customer already collects. Its guarantee is two-sided, stated in the distance a local verifier measures: any substitution shifting a single-qubit output marginal by $\delta$ in trace norm forces a contract deviation of at least $\delta/\sqrt{3}$, the constant tight and independent of qubit count; the guarantee is relative to the chosen observable family and reference-input set. For local-unitary substitutions the adversary's blind set is characterised exactly, as a commutation condition, which gives the defender a rule for choosing challenge inputs that shrinks it. A finite-shot budget rule bounds false accepts and false alarms at once, one tolerance separates attack from the benign drift observed here, and every decision enters a hash-anchored audit trail. On an IBM Heron r2 processor a substituted quantum-kernel intrusion-detection pipeline evades the weak contract and our verifier halts it, while the honest channel stays within tolerance.

[1406] arXiv:2606.15555 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Service-Induced Congestion in Memory-Constrained LLM Serving
Ruicheng Ao, Jing Dong, Gan Luo, David Simchi-Levi

Subjects: Optimization and Control (math.OC); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Machine Learning (stat.ML)

In large language model (LLM) serving, each request accumulates persistent graphics processing unit (GPU) memory during service as its key-value cache grows with every generated token. Under high concurrency, aggregate memory usage therefore increases endogenously over time: the service process itself creates future capacity pressure. When memory capacity is exceeded, systems evict active requests, discarding cached state and restarting them later, which wastes computation and reduces throughput. We develop a discrete-time dynamical model of memory-constrained LLM inference that captures admission, memory growth, and eviction under continuous batching. In the saturated-input regime, the system admits both eviction-free fixed points and limit cycles with evictions. For homogeneous workloads, we show that the eviction-free equilibrium is unstable and that, except for a Lebesgue-measure-zero exact-capture set, the system converges to a unique worst-case limit cycle that is asymptotically stable outside this exceptional set, with throughput losses as large as 50%. For heterogeneous workloads, we prove a stability criterion in the two-class common-input setting and explain how the survival-polynomial mechanism generalizes to multiple classes and heterogeneous-input lengths. Under an input-dominated scaling regime, coprime decoding lengths stabilize the eviction-free equilibrium, while non-coprime lengths create synchronized modes that drive instability. These results characterize when workload heterogeneity desynchronizes completions and helps stabilize memory-constrained serving. More broadly, we identify service-induced congestion as a structural instability mechanism and derive scheduling design principles for sustaining high throughput.

[1407] arXiv:2606.20184 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Operator learning for efficient quantum computation
